Minx En at Atandate nau was one ot tnose 'functions which are rarely affected by any- thing that happens to trouble the luckless -persons who have to appear at them. It is true that on such dreadful occasions as the night after the Earl's arrest and that yet more awful one to his relations, when he had been committed for trial, Giles and his satel- lites allowed the ladies to omit the ceremonious meal, with its many dreary courses; but such favour was not to be accorded often, and now for weeks past everything at the Hall had gone on in its usual fashion and the three ladies, though their hearts might be breaking, sat down to an elaborate meal at half-past seven. Giles went as usual to announce the formula, "Dinner is served," but this evening only two of his ladies obeyed the call and Lady Mary said to him as she rose to pass into the dining-room : " Where is Miss Jardine? I have not seen her for swe hours." "Mr. Fielding called in a fly and took Miss Jardine away, my lady," replied Giles. "That was ages ago; surely she is back by - -now."

"I beg your pardon, my lady, Mr. Fielding came a second time, saying that Miss Jardine was required at Leigh Court ; he had a hired fly, and they went away in that; he could not wait for the carriage to be brought Pannd." And Giles vanished to the side-table, where he presided over rhe dishes. Lady Mary's eyes cast an enquiring glance at her niece; she could not speak her question before the servants, but Magdalen answered her silent enquiry frankly enough. "I believe Sir John Leigh only returned from London this morning; he may have heard something/fresh there." , Dinner dragged wearily on; Giles would not spare them a single course and the two ladies spent three-quarters of an hour in torture; then Magdalen, as they rose to leave the (lining-room, took the initiative. • "Can't we have coffee in your 'little sitting- room. Aunt Mary? I am so tired, and we shall be quieter there." The coffee was brought and the door closed; Magdalen crossed the room and knelt on a low footstool by her aunt's side. " Dear," she said gently, "I am sure you are fretting about something extra to-night ; is there any fresh trouble ? I think bad news would surprise me less than good," she added frankly, "for we Jardines seem in for a spell of misfortune just now." "And have been, aver since your cousin came to England," said Lady Mary. "Oh, 'Magdalen, I may be a spiteful old woman, but I can't help wishing Helen had died instead of her friend; she has brought us only trouble:* "It is not like you, auntie, to say that. If poor Helen has brought us trouble, she has had a double share of it herself." "I can't grow fond of her," sighed Lady Mary. " I did think I loved her before Alandale's peril, but now I feel I feel as though, if he died, she will have killed him." They had argued this point often, and Magdalen tried to change the subject. " lam sure you are extra ' down ' to-night, dear ; what is wrong ? " " It's only a trifle, but it all seems to point to the same thing—deceit in Helen, How -many months is it since she came to US? " "Between five and six, but--" "Let me finish, Magdalen. This afternoon a letter came addressed I Miss Hildred Jasper I' Now, Magdalen, again and again when I asked Helen about her poor friend, whether there were no relations we ought to seek out and break the news to, she always made the same answer—that Hildred Jasper had no one belonging to her and was quite alone in the world. Now, this letter proves she spoke an untruth ; Hildred has rela- tions and they have written to her. She must have been in correspondence with them just before she left Australia or they would -not have known she was coming here.' "Where ia the letter ? " "I told Giles to give it to Helen." I " I think if I were you," said Magdalen slowly, "I would ask Helen to let me see that letter. 'I don't believe." she went on frankly, "there is anything you need blame my cousin for, but I feel sure you won't be able to help -blaming her in your heart unless you have convinced yourself that ' letter is harmless. Why, Aunt Mary, poor Miss Jasper may have had relations so humbly placed in life that she -.would keep their very existence from Helen." 1. "In that case they woul: have written sooner, if only to ask for help." "Ask to see 9-te letter,' said Magdalen gently; " nothing else will convince you that you are wronabing Helen." "I wish she would come home," said Lady Mary, going ' off to another injury. " It's nearly nine o'clock, Ma•dalen, and it's not -seemly that she should 'be wandering about at this hour." . "Mr. Fielding will take. care of her," said Magdalen; "he is quite an old friend, you know." But when ten o'clock was past, even 'Magdalen grew uneasy, and astonished her aunt by suggesting they should send a message to the Rectory. " I know Mr. Fielding meant to sleep at his father-in-law's, so we shall at least glean something from Mr. Arnot." " But who is to go ? I cannot possibly let the servants know we are uneasy about Helen."

"I will go," said Magdalen. "It is only a short walk and the moonlight will make the grounds as bright as day. Of course, I won't go alone," as Lady Mary looked horrified, "Giles shall come with me. He will only think that you have thought of something fresh to tell Mr. Fielding. Why, Aunt Mary," as the elder lady still hesitated, "do you suppose the servants don't know how des- perate things are with Alandale ? If I took messages to the Rectory at midnight they would only put it down to anxiety about Kenneth." Lady Mary shivered. "If you are going there is no use in delay," she said gravely. " I don't like it, but I see no. other way.' Magdtlen rang for Giles and told him of her errand ; five minutes later the young lady and the old servant were on their way. "I'd have taken a note and waited hours for the answer, Miss Magdalen," said Giles reproachfully, "rather than you should have come out now." "I am sure you would, Giles, but it is better for me to see Mr. Fielding ; I believe he is going back to York by the first train 'in the morning and there are one or two things I must a him." The Rector was a student and kept late hours, so, although it was nearly eleven when Giles rang the bell, the respectable man in plain liyery who opened the door declared that his master and Mr. Fielding were still up. " Sir John Leigh came in after dinner," the servant added, looking a little enquiringly at Magdalen as though to enquire whether her business with.. Mr. Fielding were private or if he should show her into the library where the three gentlemen sat,
" I am sure ' Mr. Arnot will not mind ray disturbing him," said Magdalen. "Please tet me go in to them now. I shall not need to stay a minute." _

Rawlings was a well-trained servant ind kept back his surprise, not so the three friends whose consultation she had interrupted: amazement was writ large on all their faces. "My dear child," and the Rector, who had known Magdalen all her life, as he led her to a seat in his own armchair, l` I fear some fresh trouble has brought you here." Sir John, who had a boy and girl friendship for Magdalen, put one hand on her arm as though she had been his sister.

"Cheer up," he said brightly, " there's a good time coming. But for the lateness of the hour I should have come up to tell Lady Mary myself. Of course, the law works slowly, and it may take two or three days for necessary formalities to be gone through and Alandale sel'hat liberty, but you need fear nbthing worse for him than temporary -delay—the true murderer of that wretched Norton has con- fessed his crime,land I am' going up to London to-morrow to place the confession in the hands of the prosecuting solicitors. I don't know but what it may have to go to the Home Secretary, but, anyway, Miss Magdalen, the day is ours." "Thank God."

" It's great good news," said Mr. Fielding gravely, - "but I -fancy Miss Magdalen. had some special object in coming here to-night arul we had better try and eet her mind at rest concerning it." "It is ray cousin," gasped out Mag- dalen. "Mr. Fielding, the servants say you took Helen away in a hired fly; she has never returned."

Fielding and Sir John looked at each other. The Rector was a much older man and his mind moved but slowly; besides, he was not behind the scenes and did not know the secret shared by the other two. Magdalen grew impatient at the silence. "Sir John," she cried passionately, "I can tell from your face there is Something wrong. You can't mean Kenneth's innocence will be declared at Helen's cost ? You could never call it good news' that a Jardine should confess to murder? Oh, the anxiety about Kenneth has been cruel, maddening, but at least there was no shame in our grief. Now, if Helen—"

div.head: It was Mr. Fielding who inferrupted.her.
div.p: It was Mr. Fielding who inferrupted.her.

"Your cousin Helen is as innocent as you are, Miss Jardine. I feel a keen remorse that I (I will confess the truth now) once thought her guilty." "It is all right, Magda," put in Sir John, going back to the old childish name in his excitement, "the true murderer was a young Australian, Charles Gresham, and—his con- fession is in my hands." " But where is Helen ? "

"That is what we cannot tell you," said Joe Fielding. " I take shame to myself -now that I did not remain at Leigh Court to drive Miss Jardine home, but-" "Let me cxplain," said Sir John. "Magda, the poor fellow who, stung to madness by jea,ousy, committed what is called the Mandate murder, had .been your cousin Helen's betrothed. When he returned from a voyage" (he was a sailor by calling) he heard of her changed fortunes and came to England vainly seeking her -what happened you can guess. ,But though he had taken human life, I felt sorry for Gresham, and when he lay dying, promised he should see the girl he loved once more. I brought him to the Court and ,persuaded Fielding to urge Miss Jardine to see him." '! And she consented ? "

Sir John bowed his head. "Gresham died, they tell me, with his hand in hers ; she was naturally a good deal upset and we kept her at the Court till she was calmer. I begged her to let my aunt's maid drive home with her but she insisted on gobig alone, so I myself put her into the fly." "At what time? " "Half-past seven; she should have been at Alandale by eight o'clock or earlier." "She has never come I Aunt Mary is half frantic with anxiety, and I promised her to see you and ask you where you had taken Helen," Mr. Fielding looked bewildered. "I know the flyman, he is generally to be found at Thornby Station unless he is out with a fare. He is to meet me there to-morrow (I am going from Thornby to York by an early train), to receive payment for his services to-day." - -

" Do you mean that we can hear nothing of Helen until the morning? The suspense will kill my aunt." "My dear child," interrupted the Rector gently, "what else is there to be done ? If we drove to Thprnby to-night the flyman

wonld he at his own house and we could not find him/ Joe ha 's to catch the eight o'clock train to-morrow morning; the man was to meet him at the station and receive his money. I can see no way of getting at him soonc..r."

Magdalen shuddered. "Something must have happened to Helen; what am I to tell Aunt Mary? " " 'fell her that Miss Jardine left Leigh Court at half-past seven intending to drive straight home," said Sir John. "Magda, I think you are over anxious on one point; Lady Mary has not the same love for her cousin that she bears for you, and I believe she will take - the strange disappearance of the heiress much more calmly than you imagine." Magdalen shook her head. "You forget that Helen is a Jardine, and I that. Aunt Mary loves the honour of the old name beyond aught else. God knows I don't I want to speak evil of my cousin, but Aunt I Mary will think her flight brings shaine and I disgrace upon us all." The three men could say nothing to comfort her ; they heard her words in absolute silence for in the heart of all was the firm conviction that the heiress of Alandale would bring nothing but grief and anxiety to all connected with her.
------- - • 'it' CHAPTER XXIV; "*.,' t, •

A LETTER addressed to " Hildred Jasper" in the writing of the girl her friend had believed fathoms deep beneath the ocean 1 The girk who had stolen the name and fortune of Helen Jardine 'did not need to open the letter to know what had happened; the truth flashed on her like a flash of lightning ; what seemed a miracle had really happened Ind Helen, the real Helen, lived—had been rescued after all. It was true that it Seemed little short of a miracle. since again and again it had been asserted that the particular boat in which she had a place had capsized with all its living freight. It was true that more than five months had elapsed since the wreck of the "Cygnet." and that there had been ample time for the girl to communicate with England even if she had been rescued by some sailing vessel and carried off to the remotest part of the earth. But for all that the false heiress of Alandale never hesitated, the true heiress was alive ; very soon she would follow on the heels of her letter and claim her own

Somehow the' thought of contesting the claim never entered the head of the miserable supplanter, for the latter knew perfectly that " Nell " bore a strange resemblance to some of the dead and gone Jardines, and that she would know a hundred details of her father's early life and her mother's romantic marriage which thg, pretender had never been able to recall. Again and again ,Lady Mary had ex• pressed surprise that her niece knew so little of the family history and could give such fem particulars of her father's struggles in Aus• tralia ; well, the real Helen would talk oi Aubrey Jardine by the hour together and be delighted to praise him. Twice that day had the opportunity for a full confession presented itself to the girl whc had committed so great a fraud, twice she hae, let it pass her by, and now the choice was taken from her; very soon without act or deed of hers the truth would be known far and wide: very soon she would be cast forth from Alandale Hall and branded as an imposter. Perhaps she might even be prosecuted for her fraud and be sentenced to a long term of imprisonment; anyway she would b publicly disgraced, ,and keimeth, Earl of Alandale, must tear her out of his heart, for he could . never stoop to speak of love to such an one as her. .
All this rushed through her ' brain at 'such a rate that she knew just what the odds against her itterc in three minutes, _ _

Would'she stay at the Hall to be found out? Would she linger in the home she had learned to love so well until she was thrust out from it ? No. a thousand times no, she would not stay to read the scorn in Kenneth's dark eyes, she would remember his face as she had last seen it full of love and tendesness for her ; the last time they met she had been clasped in his arms and gathered to his heart. She would not let the memory of any harsher greeting blot out that tender parting. The fly had reached the cross roads, where one path led on to Alandale Hall and the village, another (by which it had come) back to Leigh •Court, the third to Thornby Station. Helen's resolution was taken ; abruptly she caught the check string and pulled it. The driver stopped at once and dismount- ing came to the fly window. "I find I "am obliged to go to Thornby," said his passenger; " can you take me there instead of to the Hall ? " "Surely, miss." replied the man civilly. not

Nvnen racy were nearing. London she took out heippurse and counted her little stock of money ; what a pity she had not happened to have more in her pocket; she had over twenty pounds in her desk at Alandale and it , would have been useful to her ,now: Of course the crisp bank notes were not rightly hers at all, but Helen jardine'S ; still if it came to that so were the very clothes she wore. Three ,pounds ten—it would not go far; what a pity, thought poor Hildred, she was not a dog, in which case she could have been put painlessly out of existence at the Home at Battersea; why was there no lethal cham- ber for humart waifs and strays whom no .one wanted 1 How socir . would they miss. her at the Hall? .How early would the search for her begin ? Perhaps though there would be no search. Mr. , yielding might put. together her flight and Sir John Leigh's story of Charles Gresham's en- gagement—he Might find out the truth, in , which case no one would trouble to look for her at all. _ _ _ _

She had no money for hotels or cabs; besides, would an hotel take in a traveller who arrived in the small hours and had no luggage? In. her dire extremity Hildred suddenly re- membered that long ago before her marriage she had lodged with a Mrs. Smith at Brixton ; it was quite five years, nearer six, since her sojourn in Byron Road and she had left there on her wedding day, but still it was tolerably certain that if Mrs. Smith still lived she was in the same house and carrying on the same occupation. If only she could find the woman out Hildred felt she would receive her without any awkward questions, she could tell her (truly) that her marriage had turned out badly and she was a widow. She could affect to have "left her luggage at the station" and later on go out and buy a cheap box and a few indispensable toilet articles. Of course three pounds ten was not an inexhaustible capital, but she had other means at disposal; she was wearing a watch and chain and two or three I handsome rings; these-must be turned into cash, and speedily. Hildred carried out her plan—if plan it could be called. She went to the suburban station office at King's Cross as soon as it was opened and travelled by an early train to Brixton ; she breakfasted at a coffee stall and roamed about the streets till she could hope that Byron Road would be waking up to the labours of another day. By eight o'clock she was knocking at the well-remembered door, arr! it reAv seemed that at last fate favoured

Y esterday Kenneth, Lord Alandale, had been declared guilty of murder by all but a few faithful friends ; yesterday it had seemed well nigh certain he would have to pay with his life for another's crime, but to-day Hildred had the blest certainty that he would soon be released from prison with no stain on , his ancient name. _ _

Poor girl, the world would have called her a shifter,- but she was yet capable of a faithful devoted love such as some women whose " goodness " is never questioned cannot know. Probably Lord Alandale and she would never meet again, but she would go down to her grave loving him and only him. Hildred went - out soon after breakfast, avowedly to get her luggage,%ut really to buy the fewest possible wardrobe necessities with which she could pass muster. She offered Mrs. Smith a week's rent in advance, but the landlady laughed and told her there was no need for that ; if Mrs. Blake had not forgotten her all these years she was not likely to play her false now. Alone in London. utterly alone in that vast labyrinth of brick and mortar which contain so many millions of weary toilers I Hildred felt certain of one thing—that the man who wrote of the loneliness possible in the very midst of the crowd must certainly have had a suburb in view, for nowhere could a human creature be more completely isolated. It was half-past ten when she reached the main road. Brixton had "gone on" since Hildred lived there, and with its electric trams and omnibuses of every hue looked a veritable smaller edition of London itself.

But the girl who only yesterday had had a crowd of servants and carriages of her own tit her disposal did not trouble herself much about the appearance of Brixton; there was a small dingy shop well on the way to Kenning- ton where three brass balls wore suspended over the dpor, and where in times past Hil- dred had more than Once raised money on her few possessions; she was .going there nerw. Her,watck and chain had been bought by Lady Mary at York and had probably cost a good round, sum; .of her rings, two were diamonds and the other a half hoop of pearls, the last having been Lord Alandales gift ; he had said something at the time about pearls meaning tears; if the old superstition were true, he told her, he hoped they would be tears of joy. The pawnbroker was an intelligent manond knew the value of the articles offered in pledge, hnt lw was also a tolerably aood iudae of
The Examiner, Saturday, March 31, 1906.

sorry to be saved a further journey of two miles each way. He was a simple fellow enough, an excellent driver, but slow tp understand anything un- connected with his own business. If the young lady wanted to go to Thornby instead of Alandale, he saw nothing surprising in it and was quite ready to take her there. The fly reached the station five minutes before the London express was "due, and its occupant had ' time to secure a third class ticket ; she would have paid her jehu, but he told her civilly enough Mr. Fielding would settle in the morning," and perhaps she was not sorry, for her purse was not well filled and she had no speedy chance of replenishing it. There were not many people standing on the platform, and none of them knew "the young lady from Alandale Hall" ; with the thick veil drawn over her face she waited a little apart from the others till the two bright lights of the engine came in sight. She shud- dered, as she saw them; those flashing lights reminded her just a little of some monster with.fiery eyes come to bear her far away from all she loved.

She got into an empty compartment feeling thankful for the solitude: noisy talkative travelling companions would have been agony to her in her present mood. Ni" No more shams, no more lies," she told herself as the train moved slowly out of the little country station. " From this day for- ward I will bear the only name to which I have a right. I will be Hildrecl Blake, the con-' • vict's widow." She was well night heartbroken, as every throb of the engine bore her further away from the man she' loved. She had no hope left, she believed firmly that she had parted from Lord Alandale for all time; she eared absolutely nothing what happened to her now, for nothing could be more terrible than what she had gone through. to-day ; it seemed to her that she had surely tasted the bitterness of death, and that the grave itself had no further terrors for her. . .

S'ae wore a light summer dress and the night air was chill she had no wrap; nothing to put over her thin black gown, and as the night wore on she was so cold she felt almost cramped ; the carriage was hard and comfort- less. After her recent luxurious life a night journey third class was something of a hard- ship, but she never troubled about that; it seemed to Hildred Blake that nothing mattered.

her, for the door was opened by Airs. Smith herself who, in spite of the changes six Years had made, speedily recognised , her former lodger. " I am in great trouble," said the girl simply, "and I have come to London to try to earn my own living. If you have a room to let, I would rather stay with you than any- one."

"There's the top front room you can have for six shillings a week," said Mrs. Smith cheerfully ; "and; of course, you'd have your breakfast in my parlour and sit there a bit of an evening, too, if you felt disposed. But," she hesitated, and then Jaeing a woman who liked to get to the bottom of things asked plainly, "isn't Mr. Blake with you my dear?" "Oh no," answered Hildred simply. k" lost him more than four years ago." Surely it was true for, though the grave had only closed over him that summer, yet to all intents and purposes Hildred had "lost her husband when the prison walls first hal him from her sight.

"Sakes -alive I " cried Mrs. Smith, "to think of it 1 Why, you must have been a widow before you were twenty." " I studied music," said Hildred, feeling some explanation of the last few years was called for, "and got rather a good post as teacher abroad, but foreign life did not suit me and I came over this spring." Quite true except' that it is usual to speak of Australia as a " colony " instead of "foreign," but Mrs. Smith was not a well- educated woman and might have made the very same mistake through ignorance that Hildred did of set purpose.. The wanderer had some breakfast—as the meal was understood in Byron Road, a skimpy rasher of fat bacon floating in grease flanked by a thick slice of bread and a cup of rather bitter tea, Mrs. Smith being addicted to her grocer's" family mixture "at one and two the pound, which required a considerable amount of "drawing" before it acquiredthe rich dark colour she loved.

Hildred noticed the coarse fare, the tum- bled, half-clean tablecloth, the broken, ill- matching china, and thought of Alandale and the dainty meals, fine damask and beautiful porcelain and silver which were wont to ap- pear on the breakfast table there ; she gave one bitter sigh at the change between yester- day and to-day, but then a thought struck her which even in all her troubles filled her with gladness.

char.i.cier, 'silo so it never entered his head that they would be stolen. He knew a lady when he saw one, and .he summed up Hildrea's story simply to himself as "unhappy mar- riage, bad husband, ruined home." He offered twenty pounds `,` on the lot," which was quite as much as Hildred had ex- pected ; she gave her real name and address, and left the shop with a strange feeling of . relief that at least starvation was not likely to haunt her at present. " She spent about five pounds, her purchases including a cheap 'secondhand wedding ring, for the one Dick Blake had put or her finger was lying fathoms deep beneath the sea. Then soon after twelve she was ready to return to Byron Road ; all her shopping, except the wedding ring; had been done beneath one roof, an all her parcels were easily placed in the good-sized tin box which was to be sup- posed by Mrs. Smith to have accompanied her to London. She could not have the box sent home, from the, shop for that would haye be- trayed her ruse at once, lot there was a way even out of that difficulty. Cabs are plentiful in Brixton and the smart salesman who had waited on Hildred would have been quite wiliing to send for one. - " Mrs. Blake," however, preferred to go for the cab herself, and she walked briskly to- wards the nearest stand, rather hoping she might meet with a disengaged four -wheeler ,rawling along looking for a fare ; she was to . meet something else, however, which -changed the whole course of her future.

' As she walked gently towards the station, a short, thickly-set man who had been watching • he some time suddenly stepped forward and laid one large hand upon her shoulder. " Hildrecl, by all that's lucky I Don't you run away, my dear. I've a great deal to say to you." It seemed to the miserable girl that a Nemesis was always to dodge her footsteps, and that never in this troublesome world was she to know what peace meant, for the man beside her was Edwin Blake, her husband's brother and evil genius. (To be continued.)

In a week's time the wound appeared te be quite healed,and though I couldn't account for a constant pain in my leg, I turned out again the Satur- day after the,accident. div.head: SCIENCE NOTES AND NEWS.
div.p: SCIENCE NOTES AND NEWS.

GERMAN silver is a curious example of misnam- ing. For it does not contain a particle of silver, and it is not a German invention. German silver was a Chinese invention introduced into Europe by the Germans.

div.head: OONCERNING SLEEP.
div.p: OONCERNING SLEEP.

Dr. J. S. Christison tells us that the MINA and spinal cord only partially sleep, and that the greatest depth of sleep in normal persons usually occurs in the second hour, while in mentally diseased persons it commonly occurs towards the end of sleep. In narcotic sleep the senses are more completely shut to external stimuli than in normal sleep, while in hypnotic sleep the senses ara excessively active and keen. The character- istic of the sleep of coma is that respiration changes in character, becoming more shallow. Nearly 40 per cent, of persons in ordinary health between twenty and thirty years of age talk in their sleep at times, and most can answer ques:. tions while asleep. - - 'PREPARATION OF PURE STRONTIUM.

An account of the isolation of strontium, the rarest of the metals of the alkalire earths, is given by Guntz and Roederer in the Comptes Rendus de l'Aeademie des Sciences. The method which succeeded in the case of barium was also em- ployed in this instance, strontium hydride being obtained by saturating strontium amalgam with hydrogen, and then distilling off the mercury. The• hydride when heated in vaetio at I,ooodeg.C. dissociates, and the vapours of strontium are con- densed on a cooled steel tube. The product, which contains 99'43 per cent, of strontium, is a silvery white crystalline metal melting at 800deg.0., and volatilising at higher tempera- tures; it is not affected by cold dry carbon di- oxide, but dissolves in alcohol or cold water liberating hydrogen. The heat of -'oxidation of strontium is midway between those of its allies, calcium and barium.

div.head: DUST FROM FALLING STARS.
div.p: DUST FROM FALLING STARS.

It is often asked, What becomes of the vast number of falling stars which enter our atmo- sphere? It is impossible to conceive that they are utterly dissipated and vaporised in the upper regions, says Cassell's "Popular Science." The probability is that after combustion they are frittered into dust, which slowly subsides upon the earth's crust; for it has been shewn that, though many of the particles of dust that are always floating in the air rise from the soil, some display a peculiarity of composition and form strongly suggestive of a celestial origin. A fall of " cosmical dust" has been inferred from the investigations of several scientists, whose conclusions appear to be that iron is mingled with the dust that has been accumulated in church towers by the winds of ages, and that this iron, as it floats in the air, is often trapped in its fall by snow, which frequently gives traccs of it

div.head: WHAT IS A POISON?
div.p: WHAT IS A POISON?

Dr. R. G, Eccles gives some interesting infor. mation about poisons. He asserts that (1) no sub. stances are poisons per se; (2) that the idea that minute amounts of poisons are injurious is an -error; (3) that different organisms respond differ- ently to different poisons; and (4) that the quality of poiponousness is, for each particular organism, a function of dose. To know whether it is proper to consider any substance as a poison, it is neces- sary to know the animal or plant to which it is to ba administered and the dose in which it is to be given. Under sufficient dilution, so that a Is/rgo dose cannot be administered, neither ,strychnine, arsenic, nor other poison body can reasonably be considered poisons. Prussic acid, as present in fruit, is as

HARMLESS AS WATER, and all so-called poisons: under \sufficient dilu- tions become absolutely innocuous.' It has been experimentally shewn that poisonous substances, at certain definite dilutions, are not merely in- nocuous, but that they are positively beneficial. As protoplasm (that which forms the contents of the body's cells) is indifferent to slight warmth, stimulated into greater health and vigour by in- creased warmth, but killed by excessive heat, so also it behaves to poisons in a somewhat similar matter.

div.head: TREES THAT YIELD ELEMI.
div.p: TREES THAT YIELD ELEMI.

The source of the elemi of the Philippine Islands has - not hitherto been certainly known. The ,resin yielded by certain trees, elemi is a product of some commercial importance. It is used chiefly in the manufacture of spirit and turpentine varnishes, and as the constituent of a stimulating ointment it has a place in the British pharmacopceas. In the Philippines it is used for caulking ships, and kneaded with rice husks as torches. In the "Medicinal Plants" of Trimen and Bently it is described as the product of a species of Canarium, allied to Canarium Commune. Mr. E. D. Merrill Was had the op.. portunity of studying the question in the Philip- pines with the flowers and fruit and resin—locally known as "Bros. "—before him, and hd assigns °lend to the tree' Canarium luzonieum, that is, the Canarium of the island of Luzon. Other species of Canarium yield brea, but not, accord- ing to Mr. Merrill, the commercial elerni. Mexi- can and Brazilian elemi are the products of species of Icica, or incense tree. The Elemi tree, Rica elcmigera, is abundant in French Guiana.

div.head: DISTILLATION OF PLATINUM._
div.p: DISTILLATION OF PLATINUM._

The refractory metals, platinum, 4:palladium, rhodium, and iridium, were first melted by Deville and Debray in 1859, who fused them in a lime crucible by means of the heat applied directly from the oxy-hydrogen blow-pipe, this agent giving the highest temperature attainable at that time. Moissan. who had already distilled copper and gold, has also succeeded in volatilising the above metals, besides osmium and ruthe- nium, which could not be dealt with in the oxy- hydrogen flame owing to their rapid oxidation. By employing a simple form of electric furnace with a current of 500 amp6res and an E.M.P. of 110 volts, five ounces of platinum were raised to the melting point i, one or two minutes, and steady ebullition commenced in about five minutes. Iridium, ruthenium, and rhodium also boiled equally readily under similar conditions, and palladium, although more fusible than platinum, also required the same current and voltage to raise it to the boiling point. Osmium is the least volatile metal of the group, and re- quired 700 amperes with 110 volts when an ounce of distilled metal was obtained in five minutes from a sample weighing five ounces. ,A RADIUM BROMIDE EXPLOSION.

Mr. J. Precht reports, in the Physkalischc Zeitschrift, the explosion of a small glass tube containing radium brordide. The tube, 2 milli- metres in diameter, with a wall thickness of 0•5 millimetre, had been charged with 25 milli- grammes ,of radium bromide ten months pre- viously, and had been used for experiments in the calorimeter and in liquid air. An experi- ment in liquid air having been completed, the tube had been lying on the table for threo minutes, when it exploded and broke into almost microscopical fragments. The circumstances suggested a yielding to an internal pressure which Procht calculates at about twenty atmos- pheresi there was no indication that the tube had first cracked undbr temperature strain. The explosion would thus be duo to the pressure of the gaseous emanation which had accumulated during the 'ken months. Madame Curie had a similar accident a few years ago; but at the moment she was heating the tube, which had been kept sealed for two months. That a gas rushes out of radium bromide tubes, when they are opened, has repeatedly been observed.
FROGS THAT BUILD NpsTs. Mr. G. A. Boulanger has described an interest- insr fr.6l-,:s-Ased... found by Dr, SC., Christy in the

foAst of Bugomo, east ot Lake Albert. The re. mains of this nest are now to be seen in the British Museum of Natural History. It is about 41n. long, and formed of spittle-like froth hard- ened on the outside. Attached to the back of some leaves hanging some 18in. above is small' stream, it contained when found a wriggling mass of tadpoles. The species to which this nest- making frog belongs has not been ,ascertained, but Mr. Boulenger conjectures that it may be a tree frog known as "Cheiromantis Xerampe- lints," This frog is known to inhabit Uganda, and another species is known to protect its eggs, in a similar way. If the eggs are,taken from the nest and placed in water they are destroyed. This, comments the Globe, is a remarkable fact, seeing that the eggs of our native frog are laid its the water.. _ _

It is -pointed out that in Japan frogs of the genus Rhacophorus, and in South America species of Phyllomedusa, have the same nest- making habit. When the young are sufficientry developed the froth dissolves, and they drop into the water. A species of Polypedates in tropical West Africa, again, .deposits its eggs in an albu- minous mass which it attaches to the leaves of.a tree overhanging a pool or water-hole. During the rainy season the albuminous matter is soft- ened,' and the ens washed into the pool. Here they are fertilised by the male ,and develop into tadpole. Very curious, too, is the habit, of a small frog (Alytes obstetricans) found in France and Germany. The eggs are fastened together to form a long cnam, wmen tne male twines rouna his thighs. He then goes into retirement for a while. When the eggs are ready to hatch he goes into the water, and the tadpoles escape.

div.head: NATIONAL UNION OF TEACHERS.
div.p: THE NATIONAL UNION OF TEACHERS.

The National Union of Teachers which now numbers 56 County Associations 486 Local Associations, and 57,584 members, will hold its thirty-seventh annual Conference at Easter in Scarborough by invitation of the Mayor and Corporation of the Borough. There will be receptions and excursions from Thursday April 12th onwards, but the Conference proper will open on Easter Monday, April 16th, when his Worship the Mayor (Alderman W. Hastings Fo,oler,) the Borough Member of Parliament (W. Russell Rea, Esq.), the Right Hon. A. H. Dyke Acland, and other influeotial gentlemen representatives of the Borough and Corporation will welcome the visitors. Over 2,000 representatives of the branches of the Union, as well as delegates from kindred Associations at home and abroad, have been appointed to attend Conference. Mr. T. P. Sykes, M.A., the new President, will deliver , his inaugural address dealing with current questions of great educational interest. The Vice President, Treasurer, and Members of the Executive for the ensuing year will be elected, and the result of the poll for place of Conference in 1907 will be announced. The Mayor has invited the members and officers of the Executive, the officers of the Teachers' Benevolent and Orphan Fund Council, and of the Teachers' Provident Society, to n public luncheon. Debates upon the questions of Teachers' Code of Honour, School Curriculum, School Discipline, Examination of Scholars, Religious Education, Exami- nation:and Religions Tests for Teachers, Feeding of Hungry Children, Gambling, Attendance of children under five years old, Half-time Labour system, School Attendance, Special Courts for Children Teachers' Register, School Music, Promotion of Teachers, Teachers' Salaries, Size of Schools and School Depart- ments and Classes, National System of Education, and Training of Teachers will take place during the Public Sessions of Conference, and there will be Sessions for considerations of private business and matters domestic to the Union. The annual meetings of the Teachers' Benevolent and Orphan Fund, and of the Teachers' Provident Society will be held on the Thursday, and Monday respectively. A comprehensive exhibition of apparatus, books, maps, musical instruments etc. for school use will be held. The National Temperance League will entertain representatives to breakfast on the Tuesday, when Sir Victor Horsley will speak. A Conversazione will be held on the Wednesday, the Con- ference Ball on Thursday, a Ladies' "-At Home" on the Monday, and meetings of the National Federation of Assistant Teachers, the National Association of No- Collegiate Certificated Teachers, the National Federa- tion of County Teachers, the Federation of Teachers in P.T. Centre Classes, and Reunions of former training college Students will form additional features of the Conference arrangements. The Right Hon. the Countess of Londesborough will on Thursday receive the purses contributed by the various branches of the Union towards the maintenance of Orphanages and othbr benevolent institutions connected with the Union, and present the trophies awarded to the branches con- tributing the largest sum per member. An attractive programme of excursions to Robin Hood's Bay, Forgo Filey, Rievaulx Abbey. Picketing, Whitby, Scc. with shorter trips by road, rail and water will conclude what is confidently expected to be a busy and useful week.

div.head: Warrington Apollo Choir's Success. . _ _ _
div.p: Warrington Apollo Choir's Success. . _ _ _

The Warringt7ou Apollo Choir, under the conductor- ship of Mr.Berrey,have added another victory to their list by winning the first prize of £lO and a silver-mount- ed baton for the conductor offered at the Leigh Eisteddfod on Saturday. The test piece was" Song of the Crusaders." (De Rille). The adjudicator, Mr. Mangwen Davies, of London, said that the competition had been an excellent one, and that the Apollo Choir possessed a fine set of bass singers, producing a very rich tone. This choir had given him a splendid interpretation of the piece, and were very united, and deserved the prize. This is the Dith first prize won by the Apollo Choir at different eisteddfodans. At the same eisteddfod Miss May Isherwood, of Stockton Heath (pupil of Miss Ethel Dunn), was awarded the first prize in the children's solo competiti-m, the adjudicator speaking very highly of her rendering of the test piece " Time's roses." This is the second success won by Miss Isherwood, who at the recent Warrington Eisteddfod was awarded a special prize.

div.head: RESCUED WAIFS' GRATITUDE.
div.p: RESCUED WAIFS' GRATITUDE.

A very striking and gratifying instance of gratitude in humble life is reported in connection with " Mr. Fegan's Homes" in Southwark-street, S.E. For the last 22 years a party of rescued waifs has been sent to Canada. About 17 years ago some of the" old boys" in Canada joined in sending £lOB, " As a New-Year's surprise gift to Hr. Fegan, towards the support of the. old Homes." Each year since a New Year's Thank- offering has been contributed in this way, increas- ing in amount from £134 in 1903, £489 in 1901, £631 in 1905, to no less than £761 this year. Thus those poor boys, rescued in many cases from the gutter or the gaol, have now sent back towards the support of the Homes that befriended them in their time of need, a total of £s,lo3—not money collected from others, but every cent of it contributed out of their own hard-earned savings. It is also gratifying to learn that no less than 303 boys have cheerfully repaid the £lO laid out on their emigration " to help to give some other poor fellow a chance in life." Mr. Pegan is now preparing the 24th party. There are 100 well-trained boys ready and eager to start. Openings are waiting for them already in carefully chosen homesteads. There is a. Distributing Home in Toronto, and all the boys placed out are regularly visited and watched over. Many of those thus emigrated have now their own farms or have made their way into responsible positions in professional or business life. The entire cost of each boy's emigration, including ocean passage, railway fares and comfortable outfit, is only £lO.

The Examiner, Saturday, March 317 1906. WOMAN'S REALM' WARRINGTON. TEACHERS' ANNUAL Warrington Widow's Misfortune. MEETING. Mrs. Ratcliffe, a widow from Warrington, met with a great misfortfine last week end. She and her family had finished removing into 12,Lawrence-street,Eccles, THE RELIGIOUS EDUCATION at midnight on Saturday, and about an hour later, the new residence was found to be in flames. The Eccles CONTROVERSY. fire brigade was summoned but the cottage was gutted and the furniture, which was valued at 5.,200, was destroyed. Cost of Local Education. Ragged School and Mission. On Monday evening a grand concert was given in in the above room by the pupils of Lorne House School, by kind permission of the principal Miss Williams. A capital programme was submitted con- sisting of two cantatas, songs, action songs, instru- mental and piano solos, which gave great satisfaction to all present. The duties of accompanist were ably carried out by Miss Roseollar. A vote of thanks to all who had taken part, moved by Mr. Gough and seconded by Mr. Wright, brought a very enjoyable evening to a close. Underground Telegraphs, Through Warrington. The Government underground telegraph cable from St. Martin's-le-Grand to Glasgow, is now complete though two or three weeks will elapse before it is available for public traffic. The first section of the system to Birmingham has been in operation for more than four years, and it has since been pushed forward to Warrington,when subsidiary lines were constructed to Manchester, Liverpool and Leeds. From Warring- ton to Scotland the route is via Preston, Carlisle and Hamilton, the total distance being about 400 miles. ASK for CIINNDIGHAM'S HIGH-CLASs MINERAL WATERS.--AdVt. Beautiful Warrington. A meeting of the Howley Ward Committee of the Beautiful Warrington Society was held at the Old Academy on Monday evening when the following officers were elected :—Chairman, Alderman Bennett; treasurer, Mr. J. S. Hill ; and secretary, Mr. W. H. Smalley. Several suggestions were made with refer- ence to the beautifying of the ward and amongst other things it was decided to plant a few trees opposite the National School in Church-street. A proposal was also made to encourage the growth of plants in window boxes and the Committee to greatly further this form of plant growing :Vey believe it will tend very materially to beautify the ward. Funeral of the Late Master A. Fairhurst. The funeral of Master Arthur Fairhurst, aged 13, who was drowned in the Sankey and St. Helens Canal at Bewsey on March 21st, took place at the Warring- ton Cemetery on Sundiy afternoon. The funeral ser- vice was held in the Buckley-street Methodist Church which the deceased had attended. The deceased was a member of the choir and of the Band of Hope, and members of both bodies walked in procession to the Cemetery, the attendance including Mr. A. Jennings, the superintendent of the Sunday school, and Mr. A. Corney, the headmaster of Wycllffe day school. Floral tributes were sent by the choir, the scholars, Mr. Jennings, and a large number of friends. The service at the graveside, where hymns were sung, was con- ducted by the Rev. C. L. Stowe. PUBLIC BENEFIT, UNDER THE CLOCK FOR BEST BOOTS IN LANCASIIIRE.—Advt. Popular Penny Concerts. The series of popular penny concerts which have been held every Saturday night during the winter months in the Bold-street school, will conclude this Saturday everfing. Last Saturday the schoolroom was crowded to its utmost capacity, when another excellent programme was submitted. Several songs and duets were given by members of Mr. T. Brough's juvenile choir in a praiseworthy manner, whilst Mr. B. Wads- worth's juvenile choir acquitted themselves admirably in the rendering of several choruses. Mrs. Arthur Parkinson was warmly applauded for her songs, and Master J. Nurse delighted the audience with his humorous songs. Great credit is due to Mr. 'l'. Brough and Mr, B. Wadsworth for arranging such an excellent entertainment. They also acted as accompanists. Warrington Catholic Young Men's Society. The debating team attached to the above Society has just accomplished a meritorious performance by defeating last year's winners of the C.Y.M.S. Shield Competition—Our Lady Immaculate, Liverpool, in a debate held at Warrington on March 25th. The sub- ject " Should the Vaccination Penal Laws be repealed ?" afforded abundant scope for the competing teams. The Warringtonians, in stating their case for the affirmative, immediately made it evident that they were not going to attempt to dispute the decline of small-pox, but they would shew that this decrease had been brought about by a combination of improvements in sanitation, isolation, etc. In doing so the sup- porters of the affirmative showed how the death-rate from zymotic diseases other than small-pox, had declined gradually, and iii the same ratio as that of small-pox, and that therefore the condition of things which brought about the decreases must be identical. They contended that the enormous advance made in sanitation and the isolation and treatment of the disease since the days prior to vaccination, must be the cause of the declining small-pox. The Warrington men demonstrated by statistics of the British Isles that in our large towns, where there is much overcrowding and its attendant evils, the conditions are specially conduciverh otip oitpatit populated dbaoetttehf hddeteehdrediis:ppi districts of small-pox, but in more people eolmiacf and tndhinisoss cannot anetcdletierrrwii morevnaegs. at Thenaturalhwaataway the ho con- conclusionconditions,tsparselyett e slums would do away with the conditions under which all disease exists and spreads. In con- clusion, the affirmative protested against enforcing any penalty, because a person from conscieu- tious or any other reasons refused to allow the State to interfere with his individual rights and inject into the body of his child, a serum which might contain the germs of other disease. The Liver- pool men gave an extremely good aocount of them- selves, under a very able leader, who commenced by quoting figures showing the ravages of smallpox in pre-vaccination times. They did not wish to detract from the merits of sanitation and isolation but a com- parison of the statistics showing \the great decline of smallpox since Dr. Jenner's great discovery, and especially since the compulsory enforcement of vacci- nation, ought to convince their opponents that to 'vaccination and to that alone was due the present low I smallpox death rate. The negative also advocated not the repeal of the present Act, but the still further improvement of the Vaccination Laws by enforcing re-vaccination in adults. Germany was quoted ms specimen of a well vaccinated country, with a low death rate, and finally the theory of "Interference rwith individual rights " ought not to be considered where the welfare of the community was at stake. It was felt that the negative had made out an extremely good case and this was justified when the 'adjudicators announced that Warrington had gained the victory by the narrow margin of 13 points. Warrington by tins victory, win the championship of " B "Division. and hope to conclude their successful first year by holding for the next twelve months the C.Y.M.S. Shield. div.p: SECRETARY'S REPORT:

Mr. IJesoN read the following short report, which was adopted :—We commenced the year with 126 mem- bers ; we close with 118. Yet progress has tO be reported, for during the year the new association of As hton-in-Makerfield has been formed and this took from us 23 members. We have had a considerable accession of new members from the borough, while retaining ten Cheshire teachers and eight in the administrative area of Lancashire. No member has died, and only one has lapsed (a lady). I cannot let this opportunity pass without referring to the removal of one of the oldest members of this Association, and one of the most respected of the burgesses of Warrington, Mr. John Dewhurst. We all wish him long life. good health, and great peace in his retirement (Applause.) Seven teachers have joined within six months of leaving college or on obtaining their certifi- cate at half fees. Your committee cannot help regretting that this number is not greater, and appeal to the head teachers to do a little missionary work in this direction. In addition to the four general meetings which have been held according to rule, we in the early part of the year joined with the class teachers in hold- ing a united meeting, when we were addressed by the prominent local educationists. The June meeting took the form of a picnic to Dunham Park, and, although not well patronized, was most enjoyable. The Septem-. her meeting took the form of a whist driye and social evening. The interest in the work of the association,and the attendance at the meetings have been well main- tained. The committee has met on eight occasions, and with ono exception all the members have attended regularly.

div.head: FINANCIAL POSITION.
div.p: THE FINANCIAL POSITION.

A satisfactory balance sheet was presented, showing a credit balance of £2O Hs. id. Some discussion ensued as to the disposal of the balance and it was ultimately decided to set aside £lO for special purposes, a certain portion to provide an illuminated address expressing the teachers' appreciation of the long and faithful ser- vices of Mr. Upson to the association, and to grant £5 to the President and Secretary for their attenla nee as delegates at the Teachers' Conference next year.

div.head: ELECTION OF OFFICERS.
div.p: ELECTION OF OFFICERS.
Mr. WALLINGTON proposed that Mr. Kilburn,herld teacher of St. Mary's Roman Catholic Schools, Butter- market-street, be elected vice-president of the associa- tion for 1906.
This was seconded by Mr. JOHN WRIGHT and carried.

The CHAIRMAN then vacated the chair to make way I for the new president (Mr. John Upson). I Mr. UPSON on taking the chair proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. Jeffery who,hesaid,was an earnest worker, an able speaker, and one well acquainted with the work of the association. He had been officially or unofficially engaged in working for the best interests cif the Association ever since he left college and they appreciated his services very highly. (Applause) Mr. EDDEN seconded, and the motion was carried with much heartiness.

Mr. F. H. LONGSRAW was appointed secretary, Mr Upson hon. treasurer, Mr. Cann secretary of the Bene- volent and Orphan Fund. Mr. F. J. Emson press corres- pondent,and the Misses Brooks and Taylor, and Messrs. Bowen, Edden, Stansfield, and Turner, the members of the committee. THE RELIGIOUS CONTROVERSY. COST OF EDUCATION.

Mr. UPSON then delivered his presidential address. After a reference to the "furious storms of religious strife now raging," he said that in that controversy they as teachers took no part, but it was necessary to emphasize what the policy of the National Union of Teachers was. Another object of contention had arisen, especially locally, namely, the cost of education. He proposed to say something upon the religious controversy, and a few words upon the cost of education. Their policy as to religious teaching was contained in the following resolutions :—" (a) A conscience clause for all scholars or students in a school or college, residential or otherwise receiving aid from a local authority ; (b), appointment and dismissal of teachers in all schools to be in the hands of the local authority, and no teacher to suffer disabilities on account of religious beliefs ; (c) special arrangements for denominational instruction in Voluntary schools leased to or otherwise placed under the complete control of a local authority ; (d),a national system of education, based upon popular control and freed from all tests but those of character and capacity." He ventured to affirm that these resolutions contained a solution of the problem that was satisfactory to all reasonable men. The extreme men on both sides would not be satisfied with anything less than i the whole of their demands, which they would be perfectly safe in saying they would not get. Might he, with all due deference to their spiritual fathers, ask what were the results of dogmatic and dis- tinctive denominational teaching? Surely, when so much was claimed, so much stress was laid upon the , necessity for teaching creed and dogma, they were I entitled to ask : "What success has attended this work ?" They were in a position to judge. Compulsory educa- tion had been a fact for 33 years. They had a genera- tion which had passed through their elementary schools. Was this pre-eminently a church and chapel going generation? Were their places of worship thronged by working men and women, say in Warrington, where they had nothing but Voluntary schools? Was it not a subject of constant complaint from all the churches that the working man would not go to church? Were they not all continually and anxiously seeking to solve the problem of why they kept aloof from the house of God ? And yet, while that was a lamentable , fact, it was also tine that this generation was a better one, morally, than any that had preceded it. In 1867 (i.e., just prior to the Act of 1870), 19,450 crimin'als were convicted ; in 1903, 13,102 or a decrease of over 6,000. During the same time paupers had decreased by more than 220,000, and the savings bank deposits had gone up from 46 millions to 198 millions. These figures showed that this generation was more honest, law- abiding, thrifty and self-respecting than its immediate predecessor. For that improvement they as teachers claimed some credit. They held that the teachers of this country had created in their schools not a Roman Cathialic, or Anglican, or a Nonconforrutst atmosphere, ' but a moral atmosphere. Definite religious instruction was confined to 30 or 45 minutes per day, and possibly I took its place merely as one subject on the time- table, but truthfulness, honesty, purity, manli- ness, temperance, cleanliness, kindness, nonsidera- Hon for others were being taught all the day through, and all the days of the week, and surely that was what parents asked for, and What the State expected. Dealing with the cost of local educa- tion, Mr. Upson said they might profitably ask how far the ratepayer, the ratepayer whose murmur filled their ears, was synonymous with the parent. He was afraid "ratepayer" spelled "property-owner." At any rate he thought the parents would be overwhelmingly against any reduction of expenditure, if that meant any lessening 1 of ellSciency. But when expenditure upon education was ,being talked about, only one item was mentioned, and 1 that probably because it was the largest—teachers' salaries. The average salary paid to teachers in War- rington, including heads, was .£7B-30s. a week. Very , extravagant that! Again, last year the grants from ;Government and the school fees practically covered •i the teachers' salaries. The Government grants I were not paid for buildings, but for the work of the ! teachers. The municipality had to provide buildings, I fit them up with furniture and apparatus, and then the I Government said : " On the conclusion of 12 months' work by the teachers we will pay a grant." And he would say here that he was, and no doubt they were too, being constantly challenged as to whether the parents and ratepayers were getting better value in the increased efficiency of the teaching staff than they were , before the AM of 1902. But surely that Act was passed I because of the great disability under which the i Voluntary schools laboured compared with the Board I schools as to staff. It was generally accepted that the education given to the children in the Voluntary schools (half of the school popula- tion) suffered, because owing to the lack of money only partially qualified teachers could be employed. The staffs of Voluntary schools were largely composed of Arts. 50, 68, and P.T.'s. The 1902 Act,' whatever its defects, mad'e an alteration of that state of 1 things possible. The great majority of Warrington schools were badly stuffed, and now all were fairly I staffed. Was that nothing gained ? It was possible . before 1902 for a child to pass through all the standards iwithout coming under the tuition of a properly qualified teacher, unless he passed through a class taught by the I head teacher. That was now impossible. Every child i would pass the greater part of his school life under the tuition of skilled and trained teachers. Surely that was a great gain to the child, the parent, and the State. I It was also forgotten that only Bd. of the Is. oid. rate I went to elementary educr.tion ; 40. went for Secondary ' education. Severe economy was practised in the i I supply of furniture, apparatus, books, &c., only I 25., per bead being spent on these things, against an !average of between 3s. and Is. elsewhere. Expenses of I administration, school attendance officers (the number ' of whom had been increased), payment of caretakers, ! the maintenance of deaf, dumb and blind children, of ' truants and juvenile offenders, interest and repayment of loans made up the balance. Warrington bad reason to congratulate itself, not that its education rate was i high, but that it was not higher. Compared with other . county boroughs it was exceedingly low. The 1902 Act i was being administered economically and carefully,

while efficiency was kept in view. In a comparatively ' small borough such as this was and with such an enor- mous leeway to make up in the provision of school places, the burden was bound to be heavy, especially when they considered that the aqsessraen., was relatively high. Let them hope for all concerned that the eagerly anticipated Bill would make provision for increased Government grants, and would equalize the burden, so that wealthy places with a swill school population should pay their fair share of the cost, with poor and populous places—of that which, after all was said and done, should be a national charge. (Applause.) Mr. STANSFIELD proposed a vote of thanks to the President for his address, but remarked that he did not agree with all he had said. They were met as members of the N.U.T., and, he thought, ought to keep off the subject of creed and dogma as much as possible. He agreed that there was no religious difficulty in the schools, but a great many of those present were denomi- nationalists, and althoagh they had no sympathy with the strife about dogmas and creeds they maintained, as Church people, that they had not been the means of creating tilts strife. Mr. Upson had referred to the churches,and the sparse attendances,and in reply he could say that they were unable to judge offthe success of reli- gious instruction, as secular and religious teaching had always been combined in this country.lf the system were discontinued they would be be better able to gauge the effect. He was, however, perfectly certain the position in regard to the attendances at churches and chapels would have been worse if there had been no religious instruction in schools. With regard to the decrease in crime, he considered religious instruction in schools had been largely responsible for it. During the whole of the time he had been a teacher at his school he had never yet, with the exception of a Jew and Jewess, had a withdrawal from religious instruction. He agreed with the remarks which had been made about the cost of education locally. It was run on very economical lines. He did not think there was a county borough anywhere that could show more economy, and at ,the same time so mach efficiency as they had in Warrington. The people of the town were getting full value for their money. (Applause). Mr. JOHN WRIGHT seconded, and said that while he admired Mr. Upson's address, he did not agree with his views on dogmatical teaching. It would be ungrateful on the part of teachers who had been brought up in denominational schools and colleges not to maintain that system/ " For goodness sake," he concluded, " as teachers let us keep out of this turmoil of religious trouble."

Mr. E. WALLINGTON in supporting said he did not want to introduce any controversy but he would like to correct the statement which had been made over and over again that Nonconformists wished to abolish the Bible from the schools. lie thought he could state most emphatically that the vast majority of Nonconformists did not. They were as strong in support of religious instruction as Churchpeople or members of any other denomination,but what tney maintained and had main- tained for centuries was that no man ought to be com- pelled by law to maintain a religion which he did not support. They were told by some that the place for religious instruction was the Church or the Sunday school. From what he could learn the instruc- tion given in Sunday schools nowadays was of an inferior kind as compared with what obtained in the days of their fathers and grandfathers. Many children I did not get religious instruction at home and he thought that fact was an argument against dogmatic instruction, as parents apparently thought it was worthless or they were indifferent about it. Nonconformists as a body supported religious instruc- tion in the schools but there was a great difference between religious instruction and dogmatical religious instruction.

The vote was heartily accorded. Mr. UPSON in responding said he had tried to emphasise the pointthat after all they were interested only in teaching essentials. It was a good thing these storms did not come within the four walls of the schools.

div.head: DRESS-FASHION-HOMe.
div.p: DRESS-FASHION-HOMe.
THE ART OF LETTER•WRITING.

When—as seems possible—Mr. Henniker Heaton realises his dream of a universal penny postage, the art and practice of letter-writing will have received its death-blow, says Ella Hop. worth Dixon in the Lady's Pictorial. This state- ment may, at the first blush, sound a trifle para- doxical, but even the most cursory glance at the subject must convince one that from the very cheapness of the means of transit will come the decay of an amiable and graceful art. The missive which is transported to the other side of the globe for a penny is a thing which no one Friends time or trouble upon. The statements therein are of the baldest. there is seldom any attempt at epigram, ,and there is usually an air of haste over the whole performance which goes far to mitigate the pleasure with which the re- cipient breaks the seal. Letter-writing has been defined as the art of talking to friends at a dis- tance, but it must be confessed that the epistle of the twentieth century has more the air of an abrupt telephone message than of a graceful and consecutive conversation. SMART COAT AND SKIRT.

Though tho short trottoir skirt has completely disappeared as far as dressy afternoon toilets are concerned, it has retained a firm hold upon our affections as part of the neat morning costume FO much affected by Englishwomen. The smart little coat and skirt pictured in our sketch is an excellent example of the kind, and is admirably suited for country wear or for morning shop- ping in town. The material is a rough light tweed in tones of grey and white. The pretty

little coat is cut with a short basque, and some- what resembles the Russian blouse in shape, ex- cept that the waistband of soft black kid passes beneath the fronts of the coat, allowing them to hang loose. From these fronts turn back neat little revers, partially faced with striped black- and-white velvet, the collar of the coat being of plain black velvet, a distinctly novel touch. The skirt is absolutely plain, fitting plainly over the hips, but cut very full at the bottom. A panel front and line of stitching at the hem re- lieve the severity of the skirt.

div.head: NOT ALWAYS POLITE.
div.p: NOT ALWAYS POLITE.

In Vanity Fair Mrs. Neish remarks on the fact that Dr. Reich complains that Englishmen do not hold Englishwtirnen at their proper value, which, he tells us, is because we do not always exact our due. " That," she says, "is open to discussion. It is certain that some of us do not; notably the lady whom he quoted as having at- tended one of his lectures. She was a young and apparently charming woman, and she arrived late, and seeing a young man whom she knew sitting in a corner she went towards him. Ho was sit- ting on one chair, with his feet resting on the ledge of another, but he ros(., of course, and made way for her. Instead of bowinr, and taking her seat, she leant towards him, arid' said, apolo- getically : 'Are you sure you don't want that other chair for your feet?' "

div.head: USEFUL OVERALL.
div.p: A USEFUL OVERALL.

A good overall or sleeved pinafore is an in- valuable possession for the girl who likes to maintain a neat appearance while on her daily round of household duties, and more especially are these of value in this season of spring-clean- ing. There are numerous styles in which these overalls can be made, but one of the best is that shown in our sketch. It has a rounded yoke,

which may be piped and ornamented with fancy stitching; and the bodice part is put into a shaped and pointed belt, the skirt, with its big duster pocket, being also gathered on to the waistband. This close-fitting style is a trifle more elaborate to make than those that hang straight from a. yoke; but the latter kind often get in the way, since they cltag on the floor in front di- rectly the wearer stoops down. Checked zephyrs make smart-looking pinafores, but perhaps itzzt useful of all are those of spotted navy-blae or black sateen. TIIE ENTERTAINING CRAZE.

We hear so much of the peculiarities of guests, their freak-like habits, and their intolerant atti- tude towards hosts, that it must have often presented itself as a mystery, says "Miranda" in the Lady's Pictorial, that those who enter- tain have riot long ago retired in dismay from the ordeal of filling their houses with these strange beings. Now this mystery is explained. Entertaining is not only a "habit," but has be- come "second nature.' Nothing will cure us of it—not even the determined efforts of Un- mannerly guests. TO-DAY'S RECIPE.

STUFFED LOTISTELL—cut -up the meat of a fair- sized lobster into small pieces. Make a sauce of two ounces of butter and the same quantity of flour, adding by degrees suflitient milk and cream to make a thick -sauce, seasoning with salt and pepper. Add the 'lobster, a teaspoonful of finely- chopped mushrooms. the lobster coral—previously passed through a sieve—and half a teaspoonful of anted lemon rind. Mix. fill the lobster shell with the puree, cover with tine breazicrum DS and little lumps of butter, and bake in a quick oven until the top is lightly browned. Serve with bard-boiled eggs and olives stuffed with satellovi,

div.head: CONMENTIAL REPORTS.
div.p: CONMENTIAL REPORTS.
REQUEST TO THE EDUCATION COMMITTEE.

A discussion tooleplace with reference to the follow- ing resolution recently passed by the Education Com- mittee That the managers of the public elementary schools in the borough be required to obtain from the head teachers half-yearly reports upon the conduct and work of the assistant teachers in their departments,such reports to be sent to this committee after they have been considered by the managers, with any comments in reference thereto that the latter may desire to make ; the reports to be submitted to the committee as soon as possible after the 30th June and the 31st Dectnember in each year." Mr. S. W. JEFFERY said that when the Education Committee took over the supervision of the schools in Warrington they set before themselves the laudable task CIT improving the staff of the schools with the result that they had to day a greater proportion of certifi- cated and therefore more highly qualified teachers than ever there had been before. While the quality of the staff had been raised had the quality of the work detriorated ? Were not the more highly skilled teachers able to maintain the standard of excellence reached by the less qualified teachers ? Was it that the members of the committee, regretting their act of justice in providing a reasonable scale of salaries, while holding out the increase with one hand I were eagerly waiting with the other to snatch it back again ? or was it that there was a lack of confidence in the head teachers of Warrington ? He held no brief for the lazy teacher, nor did that Association desire to erect a bulwark behind which the indolent might take shelter. IThey desired, however, as members of a by no means I unimportant profession that they should be accorded professionalltreatnient. They asked from the Education Committee some manifestation of the spirit of trust, and confidence in the teachers as a body. He moved that the Education Committee be requested to add to their resolution the words : "And that the reports in all cases be shown to the teacher concerned." Mr. F. J. EMSON seconded. He said the teachers rather welcomed the reports if they could be allowed to see what was said about their work. The action of the Education Committee might be described as the first touch of" the iron hand in the velvet glove." Mr. C. TURNER moved and Mr. WALLINGTON seconded an amendment to the7effect that the Association should defer action until the Head Teachers' Association had considered the matter, with a view to a joint request being sent to the Education Committee. Both expressed themselves as being thoroughly in sympathy with the object of the original resolution. After some discussion Mr. Jeffery's motion was carried, the amendment having only three supporters. A resolution that an effort be made to get the Educa- tion Committee's resolution rescinded was withdrawn, las the Chairman did not consider it was in the realm of practical politics. I Mr. KILBURN moved that the Education Committee be asked to adopt a resolution to the following effect: " No teacher should be reported upon unfavourably until faults have been pointed out and opportunity for improvement given." There was no seconder and the proposal fell to the ground. Mr. JEFFERY'S original resolution was then carried unanimously.

div.head: EARLESTOWN LABOUR CLUB.
div.p: EARLESTOWN LABOUR CLUB.

Last week the annual meeting of the members of this dub took place Mr. W. Speakman presiding. Mr. J. W. Marsden (secretary) presented the report and accounts, showing receipts £23,expenses £l7. leaving a balance of about £6,to be devoted to furnishing and improving the interior of the premises. The Chairman congratulated the members on the result, which was gratifying when it was considered they started with no money and had a billiard table to pay for. The chief room was let to Mr. Seddon, M.P., for his election office, and they could also congratulale themselves on having been successful at the poll. The following officers were elected:— Chairman, Mr. W. Speakman; Vice-Chairman, Mr. S. Schofield ; Steward, Mr. 0. France; Secretary, Mr. J. W. Marsden, Treasurer, Mr. J. W. Thorpe ; Committee, Messrs. E. Worsley, W. Davies, P. P. Browne, W. H. Teece, J. Seddon, J. Lawson, J. French, J. Rymer, jun., and J. Hatton.

div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
JIIARCH 3let 1906.

Lord MiLivaa's good for- LORD MILNER'S tune seems to be leaving RECORD. him. Both he and his friends are injudicious. He has had the most phenomenal career of any man of his time in this country. In twenty years he has risen from a second-rate position in a news- paper office to a seat in the House of Lords. In the interval he has held high rank in the Civil Service and in the administration of Egypt. He has written an exceptionally successful book, and, under an approving and supporting Government he has made war and peace, annexed a couple of Colonies, and introduced Chinese labour into South Africa. It is really a very remarkable record. Probably there are few persons now living who will witness so sudden a rise of any individual out of an equal obscurity into a corres- ponding importance within so brief a space of time. But both Lord MILNER and his friends seem desirous to attract not less attention to his fall than was naturally concentrated on his rise. The unfortunate speech which the late High Com- missioner in South Africa delivered in the House of Lords recently, was a hasty and ill-considered defiance of the maxim, "quiets non movere," or, as we say in English, "let sleeping dogs lie." There was no public motive for the speed'. which exhibited Lord MILNER'S character in an. aspect anything but attractive. And now his friends are taking exatnple by his indiscretion to the extent of copying. The change of spirit which has come over the editorship of "Punch since Sir FRANCIS BURNAND'S retirEament is strik- ingly and almost painfully illustrated by lYft- LINLEY SARIBOURNR'S cartoon this week. The muse of History is represented in the act of requesting Lord MILNER to leave his shield with her, that it may be cleansed of its stains. Regarded in mere cold blood, this is surely a very doubtful compliment.

There are some historians who devote themselves to removing stains from soiled characters, but the process is known as " white-washing." The actual muse of History is disdainful of such proceedings: it is her business to record the stain on the shield, no less than the fashion of the armour and the grandeur of the plume. The black splash on the shield of Lord MIT.NErt is not something that has been placed there by opponents, as the artist of " Punch " would suggest. It is a very real stain ; it is something that the muse of History could not remove if she would. Still less is it litrely to be removed by the motion which Lord HALIFAX is to bring forward in the Upper Chamber, or the national testimonial which Sit' BARTLE FRERE is disposed to promote. The occasions on which the House I Lords can over-ride the views of the House of Commons are of a special character. It can send hack, it can revise, it can in many ways maltreat, it can some- times destroy the measurer, of legislation that have been carried through the representative House, 'but there its power ceases. In most other matters it is a sea breaking harmlessly against a rockbound shore. It cannot substitute its own judgment for that of the House of Commons. No motion that it may adopt reverses any motion that has been carried in the other House. It cannot by its vote destroy a Ministry; it might, in fact, vote the destruction of the Ministry every day and nobody would regard it. The motion which stands in the name of Lord HALIFAX would absolutely alter nothing if it were carried in an unanimous House. For this, and for still deeper and graver reasons, it has a certain fatuousness of character. It brings Lord MILNER again under discussion, and, however tenderly and forbearingly that subject may be treated, there can be no debate upon it which will result in Lord MarrEit's advantage. We will not here enter into the question of how far he was a factor in producing the unfortunate and ill- judged war which Mr. CLIAMBERLAIN—who was I "only bluffing," as he told Sir HENRY CAMPBELL- BANNERMAN—regards as "a feather in his cap." Wetwill not even inquire into his share in forcing the late Government into sanctioning the importa- tion of Chinamen into South Africa, under conditions which are only differentiated frora slavery by the payment of tenpence or a shilling a day and a time limit. It is sufficient to take his own fatal admission about flogging. It is only necessary to look at the actual quality of the stain on the shield to come at once to very definite conclusions as to the wisdom of putting a white- washing motion on the papers of the House of Lords. P:lo the Peers wish to proclaim them- selves in favour of ignoring treaties where they are made with such powers as those with China; to assert the right of Govenors to set aside th( instruction of the Government by which they ay appointed; to contend that when a Chinamen' been induced to work on servile terms in the mine of South Africa he may be deprived of the right of trial in open court and flogged in the recesses of the mine, or made the victims of the cangue in the compounds? If this is what it 3
