It will be " Budget night" TRH RATES. at the Council meeting on Tuesday, and the anxious ratepayer may then expect to learn what his rates • for the ensuing twelve-months will amount to. So far as we can ascertain up to the time of going to press the prospect is less gloomy than many People have imagined. It is very unlikely indeed that there will be any increase and all that the ratepayer can do is be thankful for small mercies. Possibly a continuance of the policy of strict economy which has obtained of late may result in even better tidincis a year hence. With the rates standing at 7s. 10d. in the a reduction, however Slight, would be exceedingly welcome. But it seems that we shall have to wait at least 'twelve months for any such concession.

We are glad to note TOWN COUNCIL AND that the members of the EDUCATION. Town Council have at last realised that it is incum- bent upon them as guardians of the public interests to take a real, close, and personal interest in local educational matters. Though there has bnan a majority of Town Council members on the Educa- tion Committee ever since the authority was formed, the bulk of the work has been left to the co-opted members, who in most cases have a special knowledge of education and are generally less weighted with public work. We should not like to suggest that education has suffered in con- sequence—possibly the opposite is the case—but the cost of education has increased at a rate which is alarming the ratepayers and which has aroused the Town Council to a proper sense of its responsibilities in the matter. It has to be remembered that though the Education Committee administers the Education Act, all expenditure under the head of Education has to be finally approved by the Town Council. Up to now the Council has been content, at its monthly meetings, to formally approve of "those minutes of the Education ilonnnittee which require the confirmation of this Council" without troubling itself as to the nature of those minutes. The safeguard should be in the acquaintance which a number of the in3cteu3bers have with the Education Committee's p "'fleas, but that acquaintance has been of so a nature that the confirmation of the Cerfunctory ouncil has frequently been given "in the dark " 8° to aaY- It was only when the Council blindly sanctioned the contract for the Bolton school at an excessive cost per head that the mischief of the 'practice was realized. The immediate consequence w.aa a special meetine. at which the sanction was 'withdrawn and the Education Committee's minutes referred back. The blame rests more upon the Qnuncil than upon the Education Committee, and Particularly upon those gentlemen who serve on both authorities. In its remedial measure the , Council has been quite drastic, for at the annual meeting of the Education Committee on Mon- flay the Council members placed themselves a majority upon the chief spend- ing sub-committee—the School Management 'Committee. Their action is tantamount to a !nub for the co-opted members, but in reality it anplies an admission of negligence and a measure of repentance on the part of the Council nominees. we hope they will, henceforth, devote the time and study required in evolving the many complex educational problems—at any rate until they see !low far the Education Committee is made ..InnieDendent of them under the new Act. For our ~tltt we believe that even with a popularly elected ~'.."nnational assembly the financial responsibility `gmast and will rest with the municipal authority ..4(1 Corporation.

The wordy warfare about RELIGIOUS religious instruction in the Isrsranurrox. elementary schools still continues with unabated vigour. Catholics and Anglican Churchmen stie with one another in their respective claims to special treatment, while Non-conformists look on amused at all the bother about something which has et maytetter,beeib threatened. So far, in this Nonconformist conscience has been of the eon practically silent—not because Nonconformists sre quite unconcerned about religious teaching, hut because they have more reason than other bodies to await complacently the Government measure which is at present "on the stocks." It may be that Mr. Birrell's Bill may propose to abolish definite denominational teaching from the day schools. If it does, then the outcry from the Anglicans and Catholics will be understandable, for to them religion is of greater import than educa- tion. We should not be sorry so see the complete secularization of the schools. All this turmoil and struggling over religious instruction ' does not advance religion or Christianity, and it certainly hinders education. If a course of Bible lessons will not form a basis—say a minimum basis --of agreement between the principal religious bodies then we can see no logical alternative but to disregard their dogmatical 'clamour and either insist on the bible being read solely as the word of God, or banish it from the schools altogether. In this connection we have been much interested bY the remarks of Mr. John Upson at the annual meeting of the Warrington and District Teachers' Association. Mr. Upson did not fear to touch upon controversial topics in his presidential address, and he stated plainly his belief that 35 Years oi dogmatical denominational teaching in the day schools had not advanced Christianity very far. why did not the workingman go to Church? was a pertinent question. The fact that church- going and the observance of religious formsis on the decrease are surely arguments to be put against the claim for religious teaching. It is incontest- able that public morality has greatly improved during the period quoted. but, like Mr. Upson, we do not admit that the teaching of religion in the schools is responsible for the bettered condition of things. He hits the nail on the head 'when he claims on behalf of the teachers whom he speaks so capably that " the iers of this country have created in schools not a Roman Catholic, or Anglican, at ronconforrnist atmosphere, but a moral 0,,,111. ()sphere." And we assert that they ran 0 °lntain that atmosphere at its clearest with- ever mentioning the dogma of any single b-c'et• The State has no right to place isefore its children in the schools anything more t • "an the best secular education combined with the Mculcation of moral precept.We hope the Govern- Irient will settle the religious difficulty in education relegating religion to the Churches and the IMelaY schools. There is no danger of the nation .:6vertina• to paganism and the faith in Christian- must inevitably preclude any such apprehension elthsr by Anglican, Roman Catholic, or Noncon- formist.

Medical Missions. A public meeting on behalf of the above will be held in the Parr Hall, Warrington, on Monday even- ing, April 2nd at 8 o'clock.; The chair will be taken by the Ven. Archdeacon Madden, and the speakers will include Dr. Sutton, M.p.,London Medical Mission- ary, N.W. India, and the Rev. E. J. Howson, Rector of St. Mary's, Crumpsall, Manchester, and examining chaplain to the Bishop of Liverpool. The singing , will be led by a choir under the leadership of Mr. Wilkes, organist of St. Paul's Parish Church. We trust the meeting may excel in success that of last i year.

Hill Cliffe Bazaar. A four day's bazaar in connection with Hill Cliffe Baptist Church was opened in the schoolroom on Wednesday. The object of the venture was the assist- ing of Church funds. The amount required this year to meet accumulated expenses was 50 but it was hoped by the effort to raise twice that sum and thereby obviate the necessity for holding a bazaar for two years. An excellent assortment of goods has been arranged on stalls in the schoolroom, which has been elaborately decorated and which at the opening ceremony on Wednesday presented an animated appearance.—Mr. T. Baxter presided, and the sale was opened by Mrs. H.Roberts.—On Thursday the bazaar was opened by Mrs. Forshaw, Latchford.— The sales on Wednesday realized £lO and Thursday's proceedings were equally successful.

Trades' Exhibition at Warrington. There will be numerous attractions at the forth- coming Trades' and Foods' Exhibition in the Parr Hall, and everything is being done to make it a success. It addition to the array of interesting exhibits by eminent food specialists and local trades men there will be an excellent Ladies' Concert Party which will render vocal and instrumental selections at intervals, there being a complete change of pre- gramme for each day. Cookery lectures will be given each afternoon and evening by Miss M. Small- wood, N.U.S.C. Ladies are requested to ask ques- tions and any special dish will be prepared by request. Admission is free but to prevent over- crowding a charge of 2d will be made on all children and young people in the evening. THE CYCLE of EASE is the "Premier." Prices, 7, 8, 10, 12, and 14 gnineas.—Fall stock at J. S. GARLAND'S showrooms, 51, 53, & 55, Bridge St., Warrington.—Advt. Death of Mr. George Watkins. . _

We record with regret the death which took place on Monday of Mr. George Watkins, licensee of the White Hart Hotel, Sankey-street. The deceased, who was 55 years of age, had been confined to the house for three months suffering from dropsy, and little hope I had been •ntertained from the first of his recovery. For nearly ten years Mr. and Mrs. Watkins were manager and manageress of the Conservative I Club in Sankey-street, having been selected out of a large number of candidates. They resigned two and a half years ago to take charge of the White Hart hotel. The deceased leaves a widow and two sons and two daughters to mourn his loss.—The funeral I took place at the Warrington Cemetery on Thursday amid many manifestations of regret. The chief mourners present were : —Messrs. H. and S. Watkins (sons), and J. Prosser and A. Holmes,(brothers-in-law), while there was a large attendance representative of the Conservative Club, Cycling Club and Licensed Victuallers. The officiating clergyman was the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton. Many beautiful floral tributes were placed on the grave.

Children's Gymnastic Display. The admirable work which the Warrington Gymnasium is doing was once more evidenced on Thursday evening when the children attending the classes gave their annual drill and gymnastic display. There was a large attendance, Alderman John Evans presiding. The programme was an exceptionally attractive one and the finished manner in which the various exercises were gone through showed what an excellent training the children receive. The items included dumb-bell, bar-bell and ladian club drills, ' and exhibitions on the ladder, row of rings, parallel bars, and vaulting horse. Jumping and rope climbing were interesting features and excite- ment ran high during two tugs-of-war. Mr. J Kinsley directed the exercises and was assisted by Mr. A. Mottram (assistant instructor). Miss A. Clayton presided at the piano. During an interval Mrs. Evans distributed prizes to the following : Girls' class : Ist, Miss Doris Parkinson ; 2nd, Kiss Florrie Bennett ; 3rd, Miss Alice Furnival ; boys' class :Ist, Master J. Sanders ; 2nd, Mister J. Gallon ; 3rd, Mister H. FurniVal.—At the close a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to Alderman and Mrs. Evans. div.head: ST HELENS.
div.p: ST HELENS.
ST HELENS LICENCES EXTINGUISHED

At St. Helens on Thursday, the licences of five beer- houses—Bay Horse, Legs of Man, Telegraph Vaults, Market Gate, and Brian Boru—which were reported as redundant, were dealt with by the magistrates. The first four licences were extinguished, on payment of compensation, and in the case of the Brian Bora the licence was refused.
ST. HELENS CORPORATION AND CONSUMPTION PATIENTS.

At the meeting of the St. Helens Health Committee on Wednesday, Alderman Forster presiding, a lengthy report was submitted by Dr. Buchan, medial officer, on, the inquiries he had made as to how the decision-to isolate consumptive patients in the vacant wards of the fever hospitals had been carried out at Manchester, Edinburgh and Brighton.—Mr. Brown thought people who could not pay for proper treatment and isolation had been provided for by the £30,000 which the guardians had spent in their extensive infirmary buildings.—The Chairman agreed with Mr. Brown that the guardians had been very lavish in their expenditure, perhaps too much so, and the people of St. Helens had to pay a large share, but the idea of the Health Com- mittee was to stop people going into the workhouse, and to endeavour to prevent the disease spreading, as it would through a large household where there was little accommodation and no chance of isolating a person who was a danger and source of infection to the whole household. They would prevent people being pauperised, and the present staff at Peasley Cross would practically do all that was required.—The Chair- than moved that the doctor be empowered to admit cases to the santorium on the same lines as fever patients were always admitted. When a case was reported he conferred with the doctor in attendance, and if it was desirable the patient was sent to hospital. —Sir David Gamble suggested that some terns should be fixed, and that a patient should be sent to hospital for a month in the first instance.—The Chairman said he would add to his resolution a provision that all cases he reconsidered every month, and then they could decide whether to retain or discharge them.—Sir David Gamble seconded this, and the resolution was adopted.

div.head: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.
div.p: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.

OUTRAGE AT NEWTON RAILWAY STATION. A well-known trainer-jockey George Goswell has been the victim of a remarkable outrage at Newton-lo- Willows railway station. As a Birmingham special was leaving, a passenger threw something at him, striking him on the back of the neck.—Flo experienced a burning sensation, and afterwards found he had been struck with some corrosive acid, probably vitriol. The burns were subsequently dressed by a Wrexham doctor.
ACTION FOR PERSONAL INJURY.

At the Warrington County.: Court on Thursday last, Thomas Evan Roberts, of Wargrave-road, Earlestown, brought an action against Messrs. Bennie and Thompson of Warrington, who have been making certain altera- tions to the road at Vulcan Village. The plaintiff injured himself by falling over some obstruction which had been left on the road after dark, and he claims damages. The case will be taken first after the judg- ment summonses on April sth next. MR. J. A. SEDDON, M.P., AND THE COMPENSATION BILL.

Speaking on the new Workmen's Compensation Bill in the House of Commons on Monday, Mr. J. A. Seddon, M.P., said he was more than surprised, after all the Liberal promises made at the General Election, to hear , that shop assistants were to be excluded from the Bill. The Home Secretary, it appeared, was still prepared to perpetuate a very vicious system. Why this fancy differentiation between different classes of workers? If a person worked for the profit of another, whether with hand or brain, he ought to come within the scope of the Bill. There were only two classes in the country—the ' worker and• the idler—and all workers shoule come within the provisions of a Compensation Bill passed by a Liberal Government. So far as the shop assistants were concerned he could claim to speak with first-hand experience of the changes that had taken place in the distributing trade. Many members had no conception of the great changes that had , taken place in the shops throughout the country— changes almost as violent as had taken place in any manufacturing industry. The grocery trade, with its weighing, packing, and other machines, had become almost an engineering business, and if the process went on a shop assistant would have to become a qualified engineer. "I do not want to make a long speech," said Mr. Seddon in conclusion. "I want, if I can, to imProve the rules of the house in the direction of short speeches ; but with my practical experience of the dangers of the shop assistants' calling, I appeal to the Home Secret..ry to include them within the scope of the Bill." At last the stubbornness of the Education Com- mittee has been overcome and a lady member, in the person of Mrs. Edelsten, has been appointed as by law required. It was only when the Council had twice rejected the recommendation of the Education Com- mittee to fill two vacancies by the appointment of Messrs. Jolley and May that the Committee gave way. Mr. May has been sacrificed, hut we are sure he will not resent the substitution df Mrs. Edelsten. Mean- while that lady will probably sigh for company. Quite possibly the new Education Act will result in more than one lady being placed on the administrative body in Warrington. Members of. the fair sex .have as much legitimate cause for being concerned m educa- tional affairs as they have for sitting on Boards of Guardians.

* * A remarkable letter has been addressed to the Prime Minister by 310 women now serving upon the Education Committees of County and Borough Councils, who point out how many are the matters, which are at present dealt with by authorities altogether composed of men. The supervision of girls under seven, the training of girls in the duty of housekeeping, the superintendence of female lunatic asylums, the supervision of baby farms and of mid- wives, the rules regulating the street trading of children and girls, the inspection of factories and workshops where women are employed, the treatment of the blind, the deaf, the crippled, and the mentally aflicted —these are the among the subjects specially mentioned. In the list of signatories appear a num- ber of well-known names, and we do not doubt that the letter will have been received with sympathy by the Prime Minister.

A spacial service will be held in the afternoon and in the evening the quarterly meeting of the Warrington Free Church Council and a public meeting will be held. Mersey-street Mission. On Monday last Mr. C. M. Clarke commenced his eight days' mission at the above place of worship. During the week the meetings have been fairly well attended, and through the powerful gospel addresses of Mr. Clarke a number have been converted.

Wig)life Church. The Rev. John Yè preached at both services at I this church on Sunday. In the morning his subject was: " Not self but others," and he took for his text the words: " Look not every man on his own things, but every man also on the things of others." In the even- ing he spoke on " The congregational idea of Church membership." Bewsey-road Wesley Guild- On Saturday evening a social gathering was held and formed a very suitable conclusion to a very interesting and successful session of the Wesley Guild. Tea was served at 5.30 and was enjoyed by some fifty persons. After tea a number of games were played and during the evening two members gave solos and dialect readings, and four young ladies, portraying factory girls, very creditably performed a musical dialogue with clog-dance accompaniment. The gather- ing broke up at 10.30 with a hearty" Auld lang syne."l

div.head: Presentation to Bold street Church.
div.p: Presentation to Bold street Church.

The trustees of the Bold-street Wesleyan Church, were on Sunday the recipients of a handsome present from Mrs. Af red Sileock. When the Rev. 11. G. Roberts ontered the vestry in the morning, a large pulpit Bible, a revised version of the Bible, and a hymn book were handed to him, with the request that he would use it for the first time that day. Mr. Roberts did so, and on behalf of the trustees expressed his indebtedness to the donor. A few weeks ago Mrs. Reginald Silcock pre- I sented the Church with a chair and table for the Rostrum, with an inscription to the memory of her father.

The annual choir—;;;;MonTin—C-onnection with the Buckley-street Methodist Free Church were preached on Sunday, the proceedings being very successful. The preacher was Mr. A. Truman, of Liverpool. During the day the choir creditably rendered the anthems "Come unto Me" and " 0 Israel rejoice," and Mr. J. Willett sang the solo, "The Man of Sorrows." Messrs. Cros- field's prize quartet were in attendsnce, and con- tributed " Remember me, 0 Mighty One," and "The long day closes." Miss M. Plinston presided at the organ. The afternoon's musical service was postponed owing to the death of Master Fairhurst, a member of he choir.

• Rev. Dr. Mercer's New Appointment The Roman Catholics of Warrington will, sincerely regret the departure from this town of the Rev. Dr. Mercer, 0.5.8., of St. Mary's, Buttermarket-street, who will this week-end enter upon a new sphere of work at Lostock Hall, near Preston. During the time he has laboured in Warrington the rev, gentleman has endeared himself to the congregation. He has taken a special interest in the Society of the League of the Cross, of which he has acted as chaplain. By a large circle of townspeople outsido his own Church Dr. Mercer is held in high esteem, and he has rendered valuable ser- vice as a member, of the Board of Guardians. The heartiest good wishes will go with him in his new appointment. Memorial Service. There was a crowded congregation at the Baptist Church, Golborne-street, on Sunday, when a special ser- vice was held in memory of the late Mr. John Field- house, who had been for many years an active member

and an elder of the Church. The Rev. H. Dunnico con- ducted the service, and in the course of the sermon said that their departed brother for many years acted as teacher, and superintendent of the Sunday school,and as an officer of the Church at Wolverhampton. Some 25 years ago he came to reside in Warrington, and from that day to his death had served the Church there faithfully and well. His place would not be easily filled. There was something of that old world chivalry and courtesy about him sadly lacking in the life of to-day. His private life was simple and quaint, and his religion was of that loving, trustful kind in which doubt and distrust had no place. The angel of death had visited their Church often of late, and had taken away tried and trusted servants. The service throughout was very impressive, and at the close the congregation remained standing whilst the "Dead March" was played on the organ by Mr. S. Rickers.

Latchford Wesleyan Church. With the commendable object of raising funds for the proposed new Sunday school, a tea and concert was given on Tuesday evening in the Parish Room, Latch- ford. Strenuous efforts had been put forward by the young men belonging to the Bible class, and they were rewarded by success, a very large number being present. A splendid programme had been arranged,and the following well-known artistes were heard to advantage,their efforts being highly appreciated:—Miss A. Woodland, Mr. J. Willett, Mr.E. H.Pearce, A.L.C.M., Mr. J. Gilbert, and Mr. Tom Boothroyd. Mr. E. G. Bickers ably fulfilled the duties of pianist, and the Warrington Orchestral Society's Orchestra, conducted by Mr. Tom Boothroyd, rendered selections during the evening.—Mr. Charles E. Parker, who presided, said he was very pleased to have the opportunity of associating himself with the efforts of the friends at Latchford. He had taken a special interest in Sunday school work for the last 30 years, and was glad to know they had such a good Men's Bible Class at Latchford. To make the work effective it was necessary they should have accommodation. Mr. William Silcock, said such a capital tea meeting and concert reflected great credit upon all concerned. The work in connection with the new school was making progress, and very probably in the summer, foundation stones would be laid, and the structure commenced before tho close of the present year. (Applause.)—Mr. Silcock then proposed a vote of thanks to all who had assisted to make the evening a success, and Mr. J. Mello, and Mr. J. Ditchfield sup- ported the vote which was heartily accorded. Wycliffe P.S.A. There was an open meeting of the Wycliffe Society on Sunday, when Mr. William Furness,of Great Sankey, presided and spoke upon "-personal influence." That full Church proved the influence that P.S.A.Society had upon Warrington, the lives of its members and their familes, and he ventured to say upon the morals of the town. We could not all be Prime Ministers or town Councillors, but we could all influence in some way the lives of others. Let that infleence be for good. He was pleased to introduce Mr. F. Lord, of Manchester, the speaker of the afternoon, as a grand example of one graciously influenced to lead a new life, who had , been brought from the lowest depths of sin Ito a useful worker for Christ. Mr. Frank Lord spoke upon the "Prodigal Son" and referred to the power of Christ to raise men from sin ,of the lowest type. Often in his sinful course he had plenty of money with plenty of misery, but God had i brought him to Himself. The speaker narrated his experiences with some of the lowest of the people, and he showed the power of the Gospel upon their lives. Some of these were now actively working in the Wesleyan Mission in Manchester. Mr. B. Hall and Mr. lA. Healey also took part in the meeting. Mr. W. A. , Clay sang " Behold I stand at the door " and " The Man of Sorrows." Mr. W. H. Payton presided at the organ. , The secretary welcomed seven new members, making the total 434, an increase on the membership 12 months ago. He moved a vote of sympathy and condolence with Mr. Doraville in the death of a son, aged 19, a member of their brotherhood ; also with Mr. Fairhurst, of Tanners-lane, in the loss of his son, who was drowned in Bewsey Canal a few days ago. About 370 prize books were distributed amongst the members. Address on " Labour." Interest in the Church Society Lenten addresses to men is excellently maintained and another large con- gregation assembled in the Parish Church on Friday evening to hear the Rev. Dr. Nickson's discourse on "Labour." Without going into any controversial points affecting capital and labour the preacher dealt with his topic in a way which commanded close atten- tion. The three main aspects which he emphasised were :—(1), there was the divine calling of work, (2), in such work there was a dignity and power, (3), and that there was a divine possibility and inspiration in true work. He said that if he read modern Socialistic literature aright—with much of which he was entirely in sympathy—there was one great mistake which now and again found expression,and that was that Christian- ity was opposed to the progress and aims of those who sought to ameliorate social conditions. There could be no greater mistake. It was true that in times past there had been those who from mistaken ideas had drawn rigid lines between what they called the classes and the masses, but they must remember to distinguish between false exponents of a creed and the creed itself. The history of the world showed that Christianity had dignified the toil and labour of men as no other religion had ever done before or since. The workingman if he would only have the Christ within him was the great factor in the future in social, religious, and political life. The last election had shown us that we were living in an age of transi- tion. If they rejoiced—and he for one did—that there I were signs that conventionality was giving place to reality, if it be true, as a newspaper had said, that" the first club in Europe " had disappeared and that some- thing of reality had taken its place, the great duty of every Christian man was to sea that the sons of toil and labour who represented him in the first Parliament of the world had behind them Christian ideas, Christian conceptions and Christian individuality. It was the true workman they wanted, not the mere demagogue who stood and called out some political platitude ; not the pothouse politician, who called out for liberty, equality and fraternity ; but the man who was real. This (Friday) evening the Rev. J. H. Thorpe wil speak on" Duty."

"Men or Puppets." Reply to Mr. Robert Blatehford. On Monday evening the Rev. H. G. Roberts delivered a lecture in Bold-street Wesleyan Church entitled "Men or puppets." Mr. ST. H. J. Jenkins presided over a large attendance. The Rev. H. G. ROBERTS said there was everywhere a tendency to explain the moral life of man as the pro- duct of heredity and environment. In their novels they had the romance of fatality—the tragedy of fate. The Gospel of Christ had been derided week by week as incompatible with the wisdom of the infinite ; they were told that crime was non-existent and that men and women could not sin against God. They were asked to believe that men and women in every age and in every nation whose hearts had bled in sorrow over sin, who had cried in anguish of soul

in anguish to_ for pardon' were ignorant and foolish people inventing their sufferings and imagining their forgiveness, and needing some journalist of the twentieth century to teach them that no man could really sin against God. They were asked to believe that free will was a myth invented by man to satisfy his emotion. He was told in London three weeks ago by one who knew the aspirations of the democracy perhaps as well as any man living, that there were thousands and tens of thousands of workingmen in the East end of London who accepted this religion of determinism, and who acknowledged Robert Blatchford to be their guide, philosopher, and friend, and thht if they had a desire to capture the democracy of this country for Christ it was about time they faced some of these great psychological, theological and moral problems in the light of divine revelation, and also in the light of the logic of human experience. Robert Blatchford in his book God and my neighbour," distinctly said that no man ever could sin against God and he tried to show that men were not men hut marionettes. Man, h 3 said, was the creature of heredity and environment. Mr. Roberts II contended that this doctrine of moral irresponsibility broke down as soon as it was brought to the test of individual conscience—that conscience which was the uniform characteristic of human experience. Within ourselves was the sense of right and wrong. By right and wrong we meant something entirely different from anything implied by such words as utility and prudence on one hand or weakness and ignorance on the other. Within ourselves there was something that spoke to us of goodness and badness as qualities of moral actions. He was glad to think that low as man had fallen, the wide world over we found as a rule there was some standard by which man measured right and wrong and in his (the speaker's) pessimistic moments he was glad to acknowledge that that was one of the most hopeful features in man. Mr. Roberts gave iutances which had come under his notice showing the indi- vidual consciousness of right and wrong. When we brought the scientific philosohy of determinism to the test of the indvidual conscience it failed—it came down to the around like a pack of cards. Robert Blatchford told us that we were creatures of heredity and environ- ment, and not to be blamed if we did wrong, but on another page of his work he said : " You say you have the power to choose between two MUSE'S. So you have, but that power is limited and controlled by heredity and environment." The writer plainly conceded every- thing he had been arguing against. If we had power to choose two courses that was quite enough for him (Mr. Roberts). Heredity undoubtedly was a real and power- ful force in human life. He would go so far 'as to say it very largely supplied the outtit of life, but did it determine the use we should make of it ? That was the question. rf this was determinism, the religion of moral irresponsibility, it was a determinism which could not be distinguished from free-will. Mr. Blatchford also said " I believe I am what heredity and environment made me, but I know I can make myself better or worse if I tried. I know that because I have learnt it, and the learning has been part of my environment." Then again he made the amazing statement : " He who wrongs a fellow creature wrongs himself as well and wrongs both for all eternity. I . May this awful thought keep us just." Was 1 this determinism or was it free-will ? Was it scepticism or was it Christianity ? Was it a denial of sin, or was it a recognition of the sinfulness of it and an exhortation to flee away from the wrath to come? There was not a single circumstance of our life, said Mr. Roberts, in which we had not to act as though we were free. Whether we were free or not we had to act as though we were, as was shown by the law of the country. Mr. Blatchford went on : "I do seriously mean that no man can under any circumstances be justly blamed for anything that he can say or do. That is one of my deepest convictions and I shall try very hard to prove that it is just." He (Mr. Roberts) thought that was one of the most immoral things that had been penned for the last ten years. He know Robert Blatchford was spoken of as an honest and pure man and he believed he was. He had nothing to say against Robert Blatchford. He was rather fascinated by some of the principles he presented in his socialism, but this was one of the vilest sentiments that had ever been penned and to scatter such a sentiment week by week among uneduc- cated and half-dducated and especially among young people was in his judgment not less than a crime. It was the doctrine of every coward, cur, traitor and voluptuary. Mr. Roberts continuing said that man was man and the master of his fate, and he asked his hearers not to entertain the puppet notion. It was said that the doctrine of determinism was taught by Jesus Christ. There was not a hint in all the tetching of Christ of any phase of determinism or inevitable doom. Christ's whole life was a revelation of moral freedom and His whole ministry was a ministry of moral freedom. No one was ever lost because he could not do good but only because he would not do what he could. Though much had been determined for us by causes beyond our control, one thing had not been determined and that was what we would do with our talents and gifts. His message to his hearers that night was to assert the power of their will, for they were not marionettes. The victory of character over circum- stances was one of the grandest morals of history past and present. div.head: NOTES AND NOTIONS.
div.p: NOTES AND NOTIONS.
Our congratulations to Alderman Bennett on his re-election as Chairman of the Education Committee.

A complaint has been laid against the Town Clock by the Tramways Committee, with the result that the General Purposes Committee has resolved that the clock be put in proper order and kept properly lighted. There will not, perhaps, be so many trams missed in future !

* * * Of Mr. Balfour's descent from King Robert 11. of Scotland a good deal has been heard lately. It is claimed, however, for his successor in the Premiership that not alone has " C. 8." descent from the grandson of the victor of Bannockburn, but from Bruce's enemy Edward 1., through the Fair Maid of Kent. *s* There has been a noticeable change for the better in the contour of Bridge-street during tho past week. The surrounding pavement has been almost raised to the level of the "mountain range " which we mentioned a week ago, and traffic° is not exposed to quite the same dangers and difficulties. We have only one fault to find with the Tramway's Committee's scheme of things. They are making , Bridge-street steeper instead of lessening the gradient.

"To judge from anti-vivisectionists' utterances about each other, they are animated by a spirit which can scarcely be called philanthropic. A meeting of Mr. Coleridge, Mr. Sidney Trist, secretary of the London Anti-vivisection Society, Dr. Hadwen, honorary treasurer of the British Union for the aboli- tion of Vivisection, and Mr. F. E. Pirkie, treasurer of the Canine Defence League, would need strict police supervision if bloodshed were to be avoided."— "British Medical Journal." The Borough Treasurer has reported on the com- pletion of the new borough valuation list based on the altered scale for the assessing of cottage property. On the new list the rateable value of the Borough will be £257,983, an increase of £2,472. Of this sum £2,378 represents the increase on Corporation under- takings, leaving only £94 of an increase for the rest of the borough. If the first scale of the Assessment , Committee had been adopted instead of the new valua- tion, the rateable value of the borough would have been over £4,500 higher. The Borough Surveyor also reports that owners of cottage property have recouped themselves for the increased rates they have had to pay in the last three years, by raising the rents of some 2,800 houses.

* * The father of the boy who was recently the victim of such a sad drowning fatality in the Nwsev Canal makes a suggestion in another column which is worthy of serious consideration. He points out the lack of life-saving apparatus on our small canals and we agree with him that it would be advisable, and should be possible, for life-buoys to be fixed near the turn-bridges. Similar precautions are taken in the neighbourhood of our large rivers and the Ship Canal. But the size of the waterway has nothing to do with the danger involved. It is just as easy to be drowned in a small canal as in a big one, and we hope Mr. Fairhurst's suggestion will be brought to the notice of the responsible authorities.

Notice. The Warrington "Examiner" is now published on Friday afternoon, price one penny, and is on sale at the various newsagents at about 4 o'clock. Should any difficulty be experienced in getting the paper the proprietors will undertake to deliver a copy at any address in Warrington by 5 o'clock on Friday after- noon without extra charge. UNDER THE CLOCK for Good;Boors.—Advt. The Cycling Club. The Cycling Club open their season to-day (Satur- day), with a run to Warburton. On Thursday evening there was a large attendance at a smoking concert held at the Patten Arms Hotel and the affair proved a great success. 3, R. WOOD, Piano Dealer and Tuner,Friars Gate, and 47, Old London-road., Stockton Heath.—Advt• Warrington Grocers' Dinner. The fifth annual dinner in connection with the Warrington and District Grocers' and Provision Dealers Association was held at the King's Cafe on Thursday evening. The proceedings were well attended and were under the Chairmanship of Mr. John Gandy, the president of the Association. An excellent repast was served after which the evening was spent in speecnmaking and music. Songs were contributed with effect by : Messrs. W. H. Owen, Lenton, Sharpley, and J. J. Smith, Mr. T. Taylor acted as accompanist. Silver-street Girls' Club. Owing to the, kindness of various friends interested in the Girls' Club at Silver-street, a tea was arranged and given on Monday night. About GO girls enjoyed the refreshments provided. The following ladies assisted at the tea and the entertainment afterwards:— Mrs. F. Griffiths, Miss Ashdown, Miss M. Pierpoint, Miss G-. Jones, Miss Pitt, the Misses N. and Norah Fairclough, Miss Walker, and Mr. H. M. Ashton who gave some humorous recitations which greatly delighted the girls. PUBLIC BENEFIT.—UNDER THE CLOCK FOR BEST

A BOOTS IN LANCASIIIRE.-2,dVt. Liberal Association Secretaryship. We are informed that Mr. Edmund Osborne, who was invited to become hon. secretary of the Warrington Liberal Association in succession to Hr. C. Jackson Holmes, has sent a letter to the Chairman of the Association in which he declines the office. In the course of his letter Mr. Osborne says : " Apart from the time which the duties would necessarily involve I would much prefer to remain a student of politics, enjoying full liberty of thought and action, and that would in some measure, be denied me if I consented to act in on official capacity."—We are sure that Mr. Osborne's decision will be regretted, and we hope he may be induced to reconsider the matter. LAWN MOWERS, Garden Rollers, Garden Toola, Lawn Mower repairs a speciality.—J. S. GARLAND, 51,Bridge St., Warrington.—Advt. Beautifying Latchford. A Meeting waA held in the Wash Lane School, Latchford, on Monday evening, to form a Latchford Ward branch of the Beautiful Warrington Society. Mr. I.T. Williams was announced to preside, but was prevented from being present owing to indisposition. Mr. F. R. Boberts took.the chair, and introduced the deputation from the parent society, viz., the Rev. Harvey Cook, Mr. L. Greening, and Mr. John Fair- hurst (hon. secretary). These gentlemen explained the objects of the Society, and pointed out that Latch- ford was the best part of the town for carrying out the ideas of the Beautiful Warrington Society. It had more gardens and open spaces, and it was felt that the district could be made very attractive by the endeavours of its residents. Subsequently the follow- inn g3ntlemen were appointed as the committee for Latehford Ward : Messrs. I. T. Williams, John Fair- dough, Limb, Cliffe, D. Johnson, Bediard, Stringer, Blease, Seabury, Councillor Ellison and Councillor Wilson.

div.p: My Dear Children,— As promised last week, I now give Par- ticulars of our grand Flower Show. I am -very glad that so many of you are entering for this competition, which I am sure you will find very interesting. The youngest among you stands just as much chance of winning a prize as the oldest. The names of the seeds tb be planted are as follows: Sweet Peas, Mignonette, Nas- turtiums, Pansies, and Dwarf Sunflowers. These are to be planted any time from the beginning of April to Easter. You must choose a rather , damp day,. and wait for a little time before planting, if the weather should be very cold. Penny packets of these seeds must be bought, and in each packet you will find there is a printed label giving full directions, and these must be carefully read and followed out. Try and plant the seeds in a fairly sunny spot, and, when once they begin to show above the ground, you must watch them, as snails and slugs are very fond of eating the young. green. Care must also be taken to water the plants, as they will not stand too much dryness. Later on I will give you the date to send- tile a few specimen flowers, and the senders of the finest blooms will be awarded the prizes. I hope that you Will all join this easy and very interesting competition. Some 'of you seem to think that I intend supply- ing the seeds. This is a mistake, and I think you will all be able to buy, at all events, some of the above-mentioned seeds. Many of -3,0 u send me letters with only a halfpenny stamp on the envelope. This means that I have to pay, on receiving your letter, one penny. In future all letters, except those left by hand, must have a penny stamp affixed, otherwise they will be refused. Another little thing I wish to mention is that some of you ask me for membership forms, but do not enclose -a . stamped envelope, as I asked you to do ; so, unless you do this, I cannot forward the forms. I ant glad all those who received prizes lost week are ,so pleased with them. I shall .award another prize next week for the best short. story; so you must all have a try for this prize. With all good wishes from 'UNCLE NED.

Dear Uncle Ned,—Seeing that you have got so many nephews and nieces to join your League, I should like to be a niece too. lam very much interested in the "Children's Corner," and I am looking for- ward to seeing my name in print. My father has just taken in the paper, and, as soon as I Faw a coluraft for children. I. was de- lighted. Please, Uncle Ned, will you send me a form, so that I can get twenty-four members to join, as I think you deserve it for taking so many pains in the " Corner." Soon I will send in a piece of poetry to you. I am twelve years of age, and in the stanc'ard at school. I belong to the 13and of Hope, and we have an entertain- ment at the end of the season. Last year got a medal for three years' regular attend- ance. lam captain this Year. Now I must close my letter, with much love and success to the League.rrom ,-our loving niece. GRACE AMY FRENCH.

Dear Uncle Ned,—l should like to know what seeds are required for your Flower Show. I am pleased to see what a lot of members there are now. The letter from Constantinople was very interesting, and. I liked the story of "I.The Brave Fireman." I hope my story, " Quite a Big Surprise," was among those you liked, for I tried to make it nice and interesting. I shall be glad- when the doctor says I can go into the garden again (I think I told you in my last letter • that I have been ill). I hope you will like this letter, and that you will excuse my very bad writing. lam glad that the spring and summer will 'soon be here. Now I must close, with love from CONNIE SAUNDERS.
THE THREE FISHES. Chapter IV.—Bill's Last Wish.

Now we come to the last .Chapter. The king 'of the Seawater mackerels heard of - Bill's doings. and came to ask his aid in rescuing his daughter from a shark that was going to eat her if he did not supply him with 500 fish daily. Bill, set out with his last wish used on the princess. When he had told the „shark his business, it swallowed him whole, and, with a grin, said, "So you've come to save the princess, have you? Methinks you've come to give me a meal." In a few minutes .the shark grinned again, and said; as he swallowed a swordfish in two bites, "There's another gone to my collection." Suddenly a sword was thrust
ging
the stomach .of the shark right out

ito the water, killing it. Then Bill came out through the hole made by the sword. Now, I suppos2 you wonder where the sword came from, and who did it. Well, when Bill was inside the shark's stomach, he tried to bite, but he couldn't because the stomach was greasy; so, when the swordfish came down, he took the sword in his teeth, and, with marvellous strength, thrust it right through the shark—and the rest you know. Thus tge princess was saved. The king was so delighted with Bill that he gave him his daughter's hand in marriage. Finale.

Time has rolled by, and now William Mackerel, as he sits on his throne, with his wife, reading the paper, says, "Well, I declare they've got my history in the 'Children's Corner.' Why, it's the best newspaper going." So now we leave Bill, rich and happy, for he has been proclaimed king of the mackerels in Seawater. (The End.) FITZROY LOVELL.

Dear Uncle Ned,—l hope you will be pleased with my story. I hope, you are well. I was very pleased when I.,saw that you had over 2,000 members. I fiever heard of an uncle who had over 2,000 nephews and nieces before. I think there will be room for my story, which is called

, "PERSEVERANCE." "Indeed, I cannot do all this long piece of work this afternoon, mother," said Mar- garet, quite sorrowfully. "It is so late, and 1 want to go and see those little girls at Aunt Mary's." "You cannot go to your Aunt Mary's, Margaret, till your work is finished. You do not know, my child, how great things may be accomplished by in- dustry and perseverance. Sit still, and d 9 not go rubning about from one thing to another, as you do sometimes, and your work will be done, you will see, in time." "Indeed, it is quite impossible, mother," Margaret replied, her eyes filling with tears• that were just ready to floy. But her mother had left the room and Margaret feared that it was in vain she had hoped to enjoy the expected pleasure. She held up the hope- less task before her. "All this seam to sew, and thea so many yards to hem. I, cannot get it done; it is impossible," she again re- peated, as she let it fall in despair. But, after a few moments' reflection, she took it up, and very sadly sat down to work. Mar- garet worked on steadily, and she was soon surprised to find that she had so much done; and she determined to sit still, as her mother had .said, and see, how nearly she could finish her work. Soon her brother Charles came in. "Make haste, Margaret," said he, "and see this parade in the street; it is very fine indeed." Margaret wished to go very much; but she looked at her work, and replied that she was very busy and he must excuse her. Charles laughed, and went without her. Her little sister then invited her to come and play with her, and dress her new waxen doll. But Margaret did not rise from her seat, and before the appointed time she had the pleasure of taking her work to her mother entirely finished. "I am glad to see, lily dear child," said her mother, "that you have thus conquered the natural indolence and restlessness of your disposition. I knew you could do what I asked you in good time, if you would try. I wished ..you to go to your Aunt Mary's, as the little girls you will see there are the daughters of an old friend of mine. And now, as you have felt satisfaction in exert- ing yourself to do well, I hope you will never forget this afternoon's lesson. From your faithful nephew, FRED GREENWOOD. : •-•-•

MORNING JOY. Sing. little love-birds, sing, The day is begun; Through the trembling green leaves Is shining the sun. The night has departed, The shadows have fled, And .gladness and singing Are coming instead. Sing, little love-birds, sing, The night may belong; But it passes at length • •- To the sound of your song. Though sorrow may linger, It is not aye; With gladnes,; and singing There breaketh the day. FLORENCE McEIVAN:.

div.head: BOWLING.
div.p: BOWLING.
Works' Association.
_ The annual meeting of the Warrington Works' Bowling Association was held at the King and Queen Hotel on Monday evening, Mr. J. Willett presiding over a good attendance.
FINANCIA L. The TREASURER (Mr. George Holbrook) presented a satisfactory balance sheet. The total income WRS £44 7s. 10d., and the season closed with a balance in the bank of 12s. 7d. - . .
Mr. GEORGE BALL commented mpon the fact that a deficiency last yesr had been turned into a credit balance this year. Their position, he thought, was a happy one. The accounts were unanimously passed.

NEW GREEN SELECTED, It was reported that the new landlord of the King and Queen was unable to place the green at their disposal this season and that offers had been received from the Farmers' Arms, Fearnhead, The Stocks, Padgate, and the Bowling Green, Liverpool-road, to hold the tourna- ment on their greens. A considerable discussion took place on the advisability of going out of the borough,as the landlord of The Stocks had offered the best terms. The general opinion was,however,in favour of the Bank Quay green as being the most convenient and a ballot was taken with the following result :—For Bank Quay, 13; for Padgate Stocks, 8; for Fearnhead, 0. Bank Quay is,therefore,the scene of the coming season's tournaments.

DROPSY, BRIGHT'S DISEASE AND HEART WEAKNESS.
Unable to Work for 32 Weeks. -- Cured by Veno's Seaweed Tonic.

Mr. JOHN MACMILLAN, 15, Commercial Street, Bridgend, Perth. writes June 30th, 1905 :—" At the beginning of June, 1904, I got a severe chill on the kidneys, and after a lone attendarle of two doctors, I ,was told it was 'Bright's disease. I had also great weak- ness of the heart, and suffered terribly from dropsy. When th e first doctor stopped coming, we sent for another, but he had not been attending me long, when he said there was not mncA hope; so I stopped his treatment, and took 'STENO'S SEAWEED TONIC. That was in February last ; MR. MACMILLAN ((rom Photo) since then it has done

for me what two doctors did not do in nearly a year. I was off work 32 weeks, but lam now able to continue my work daily, and I am about as well as ever I was, except for a little swelling in the legs." div.p: on that committee instead of having to do it at Council meetings. After some discussion as to the form which the reso- lution should take, the MAYonproposed and Councillor WILKINSON seconded that the committee should consist of twelve membv-s.

I Mr. H. ROBERT'S said that if they could escape the possibilities of internecine warfare by a compromise it was extremely desirable in the interests of education that it should be done. He saggested that the best course would be to add the names of eight aiditional members of the Corporation to the committee and thus give the Council the majority. In that way they would avoid the invidiousness of rejecting four men who had worked assiduously in the interests of educa- tion—aad that was what the committee was in existence for. It was not to gratify any parsonal or narrow- minded view of the question. They were there to administer the Education Act in the very best interests of the town. If they could do that, and at the same time gratify the desire of the Corporation to bave a majority on the committee, it seemed to him a far better way than that suggested by the Mayor. The MAYOR declined to withdraw his proposal He said the committee was overvreighted with co-opted members.

Mr. ROBERTS said the Corporation was solely respon- sible for the fact that it had not a majority on any particular sub-committee. It had been by accident and not by design that the majority of the School Manage- ment Committee had consisted of co-opted members. A great many of the 00-opted members had been sped- !Wally appointed to represent direct educaLional instru- ment [Mies in the town—which Mr. Roberts proceeded to detail.

The MAYOR: You have forgotten the Corporation. Mr. ROBERTS : It would be a very difficult matter to forget the Corporation,especially when you are so often reminded by its chief representative of its existence— and in the way we are reminded too. lam not forgetting the Corporation. (Laughter.) Continuing,Mr. Roberts ,said they were there to represent education and no 'other interests. They had no right to allow an- other consideration to influence their judgment or their vote in regard to the appointment of Committees. He demurred absolutely to the Mayor's statements with regard to the expenditure of the 'School Management Committee. He had occasion the other night to differ very strongly from an extremely wild and unjustifiable assertion which the Mayor made with regard to expenditure. The Mayor had not the "shadow of a shade of a tittle of evidence" in support of his statement. _

The MAYOR: Oaly what Mr. Murray gave me. Mr. ROBERTS: Mr. Murray gave you no such information. He could not give it to you. The MAYOR: Well, he led me wrong. Mr. ROBERTS: Ile did not. You led yourself wrong. The statement was made that cntain proposals of a sub-committee would involve an expenditure of 0,500. The MAYOR: £2,400. Mr. ROBERTS: The tied £lOO was the amount involved after two years and not immediately as sug- gested by you. The Mayor has made another statement it to auwnsaiegsdhtthte which elra returning of certain plans in cthivsaegclaunaclelyo wild and erroneous. He said f this committee which has regard , to schools. '. The MAYOR : I did not. Mr. ROBERTS : If you did not I misunderstood c , you. i The MAYOR : I rise to a point of order. It is not true. The discussion was proceeding when the Chairman Interposed with a request to the speakers not toluse harsh language. Mr, ROBERTS : I am in the habit of meting out what I get. If the Mayor treats me in a proper spirit, he will get similar treatment. Another statement he made which is equally fallacious is that we have begun allowing certain mistresses three months' leave of absence. He says it began with one case and now amounts to ten, and that it means £6OO a year. I bold the Mayor responsible for that statement and I say it is note fact. If it were true that there were ten cases, it would not be £6OO a year. The MAYOR: Mr. Murray himself told me that he could stand it if there was one case but when it got to ten_he thought it was a little " above board."

Mr. ROBE-BTS: He may have told you that but he never told you-the cost was £6OO a year. The rVIAYOR: I worked it out myself. Mr. ROBERTS: It shows how utterly fallacious your working out of figures is.

The 'd FiAIRM A. : I cannot allow any trgument across the table. Mr. Roberts : When the Mayor or anyone else gets up to make statements involving figures it is only fair to the interests involved that they should be accurate. The CHAIRMAN: I don't object to that in the least. Mr. ROBARTS: I wish to address myself to certain which if fo important correct remarkswowould awhhaivc eh tah e justifiably MayorMayor h ma s madepor important bearing on the result of this meeting. The granting of to such women who are certified to be unfit for duty is only what any reasonably humane- minded employer would deal out to his employees under similar conditions. I know of no occupation which to a nervous, highly-strung and sensitive woman is so trying physically and otherwise as that of a school viycehim of absence mistress, and we know there are numbers of cas es of women who work almost until they have to drop. These fora cases that we are dealing with are cases of women who have run themselves down to such a pitch that they are liable to permanent injury to health if they do not have a reasonable time in which to recover. We have given them a reasonable time and we are told that it is an improper thing to do. If it is,l am going to continue to do it as long as I have the opportunity to to do it on similar line-. It is not fair and just to come nd accuse a committee of reckless extravagance to the amount of £6OO a year—which is not a fact—when the expenditure deals with cases of this kind. Another statement the Mayor made is equally unreliable. I challenge him to give evidence to prove that the Com- mittee ever undertook to carry on the education of the town on a sd. rate. The statement has never been made, and he can find no proof of its having been made. He says we have gone from Bd. to is. 3d. and that we have not stopped. Well, we are only doing what we are compelled by law to do. (" Question.") We are only carrying out the law as I understand it. There is always an appeal to a hi her authority—the Board of Education. Up to now so far as any question of expenditure is concernsd we have always gone on the lines of least resistance. We have simply asked from this tows—l am speaking only from my own short experience on the committee—the amount of money which would comply with the minimum require- ments of the Bbard of Education in every department. , We have had to do that. If they do get a majority on the committee for the Corporation, on what ground can they curtail the number at the expense of the co-opted members sent there specially by certain bodies? There can be nothing to support such a , position except sheer cussedness. Mr. C. E. Pentrfia thought it would be a great pity if the Mayor's proposal were carried, although it might be desirable for the Town Council to have a majority. The co-opted members were elected because of their special knowledge of education and he had really been astonished and pleased with the detailed knowledge which the various members of the committee displayed of educational needs. While he _would not like to

disi;a-r-iiiii—th-e—abilitieS and knowledge of the Town Council they must remember that the members of that body were elected on issues altogether different and apart from education. The first requisite in a Town Councillor was that he should keep down the rates— (laughter)—and he should also have a knowledge of drains and setts and of the compounding of engines. (Laughter.) The question of education, however, hardly came up in the election of a Councillor. Mr. C. H. LifiswouTir said the committee had been accused of spending the money of the ratepayers extravagantly. He contended that they had not rpent I any of the ratepayers' money. All they had dons was to recommend certain expenditure to the Education COM- mittee and the Town Council had afterwards to confirm it or otherwise. If there had been excessive expenditure' the Town Council were to blame, but he denied that such expenditure had been incurred. When they looked at neighbouring towns he did not suppose they could find another that was bettor off than Was- rington with regard to the aucation rate. The Rev. FATHER WiLsoN said it was at times rather difficult to get members to serve on the sub-committees. , If the committee were increased it would perhaps tend •to lessen the work of individuals. He d not think the Committee had been extravagant andihe felt very confident that the expenditure was not likely to be diminished, who-over constituted the committee.

The MAYOR at this Point agreed to increase i‘ce num- ber to form the committee to fifteen, remarking that he wished the committee to be able to light its battles out there instead of doe or two having to face it all in the Council. Some members of the Education Committee were so narrow-minded that they were not broad enough for the whole community. As to the question of teachers being granted long leave, he had been told the com- mittee erred on the side of seatiment,but with the rate- payers it was no sentiment-7 it was pay or go to. gaol. (Laughter). His whole object was to save friction on

He did not think any of the vituperation which had been imported into the discussion was required. When the School Management Committee. was formed there were more Town Councillors on it than at present, but when vacancies occurred they were filled by co-opted members. The Rev..TonN YONGE said there ought to be a proper representation on the School Management Committee of all the educational agencies whkh were represented on the General Committee.

Mr. PLINSTON said he was pleased at the seeming desire of the Council members to do some work because he noticed many of them did not attend the Education Committee meetings very regularly. (Hear' hears) The increased expenditure was largely due to the scale of teachers' salaries which the Council itself had approved. Councillor MAGINN thought the Mayor had not been quite understood. The point was, that the Council desired to control the rates, and they had a right to, because the education of the town was put into their hands before the co-optative members were thought of. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) As to the people who gave three months.' holiday, he would lil-e to ink if teachets put in more hours than lady workers in other branches of work in the town. Did those who were so kind and genetous with the rates act the same to their own female staff, and give them three months' holiday with pay when they were run down? There had been a big cry about the large ratepayers, but he would ask who they were? Mr. H. ROBERTS: Hear, hear. Councillor MAGINN : Not the limited liability com- panies who pay the rates out of their dividends,but the poor ratepayers who pay them out of their own pocket: . It was then decided by a vote that the committee should consist of 15 members, another amendment by Mr. Roberts to increase the number to nineteen being defeated.

_ Councillor WILKINSON then proposed that the follow- ing form the fifteen :—Councillors Joseph, Craik, Evanr, Barton, Pemberton, Brough, Burton, Lord, and Wilkin- son (9) ; and Canon Stevenson, Father Wilson, the Rev. John Yonge, and Messrs. Parker, Roberts and Upson (6). The MAYOR seconded.

Seeing that some gentlemen were anxious to work and to do their duty he thought those managers who would not work ought not to be re-appointed,but should be succeeded by those who would look after the interests of the school.

ROUND THE EMPIRE. In this week's "World "commences a .striking series of articles under the aliove general heading, .which will be continued as nearly as possible at fortnightly inter- vals for the next few months. These letters will be specially written by an expert member of "The World" staff from the chief points of strategical and commercial importance along the main highway round the Emipire.. Travelling via the Mediterranean Sea,the Suez Canal, and Aden to Singapore, Hong Kong, and Shanghai, and thence to Japan and home by way of Canada, the writer will visit in turn the principal British ports along the world's highway, and will for- ward front each of them a candid record of what he has seen and hesrd during his stay. The possibility of keeping communications open along this line between England and Japan in the event of a great maritime, war, and the strategical conditions which would in that case prevail in the Mediterranean Sea, the Suez Canal, the Red Sea, the Persian Gulf, and the Pacific Ocean, will be carefully examined in the course of the letters. Reference will also be made to the war- strength of our allies in the Far East, together with the military resources of Canada—the oldest of our Colonies—and, finally, the whole. question of the pro- tection and expansion of the Empire's trade, in so far es it is dependent on the safeguarding of the highway round the Empire, will be carefully considered. The article in the present number is dated from Gibraltar, and is entitled "The Front Door of the Mediterranean"; while another is promised next week.

div.head: 1900 N.C.U. Licenses.
div.p: 1900 N.C.U. Licenses.

The action of the National Cyclists' Union in regard to the issue of licences for the 1906 lacing season has occasioned much comment and a great deal of speculation. Some riders have been refused licences, and statements as to what Will happen in the case pa others are .rather freely hazarded. It seems a pity that some better system eanyot be devised which would prevent the best riders—who always give the public a show for their money—from being relegated to the professional ranks just when they get to the zenith a their powers.

Widnes.

There was onlr a moderate crowd of about 3,000 people at Warrington on Saturday, and very few followed the unsuccessful Widnes team. The latter have had a bad season and could expect nothing but defeat at, Warrington. Fine weather prevailed, and the teams lined up as follows : Warrington—Berry, back; Fish, Isherwood, Jordan and Harris, three-quarter backs ; Lees and Lambert, b,alf backs ; Preston, Heath, Harmer, Swift, Belton, Thomas, Naylor and Shugars, forwards. Widnes—Tilley, back; Wailing, Whelan Dunn and Peacock, three-quarter backs ; Noon and J. Taylor, half backs ; S. Aspey, J. Aspey, Cockram Carr, Turner, Rigby, Webster, and Whitefield, forwairds. Referee, Mr. T. King, Salford ; touch judges, Messrs. J. Cross, St. Helens, and J. Davies, Flixton. Widnes opened strongly with the advantage of the wind and for some time carried on operations in the Warrington half. The home team came near scoring more than once, but it was not until S. Aspey nearly got over for Widnes that the Warrington men really showed resolute football. Smart passing left Fish in possession and the wing man cross-kicked when hemmed in. Tilley was caught out of place and in the race for the ball Isherwood scored a try which Berry failed to convert. Warrington maintained the aggressive, and after Harris had twice failed to make use of good opportunities, Thomas snapped up a I loose ball and crossed at the corner, Preston making a I fair attempt at goal. Half-time : Warrington, two tries (six points) ; Widnes, nil. Turning round, Preston's re-start was ably met by Tilly, and Fish's exchange gave Warrington the advan- tage. The" Wirepullers " forced the pace, and Widnes early showed signs of inabilitlsto cope with the opposi- tion, and Lambert made an opening for Thomas, who easily completed the try. Fish added the goal. Faulty play by the home backs was taken advantage of by Peacock and Dunn, and momentarily Widnes attacked. Pressing hard, the locals were penalized, and Tilley added a goal. War- rington now bad much the best of it, and the forwards easily defeating the Widnes eight, the game rarely escaped the "Chemicals'" quarters. Isherwood ran brilliantly through the Widnes backs, and passed to Harmer, As ho got over near the posts for Fish to add a goal. A characteristic run by Fish was loudly applauded and after feigning to pass to Isherwood, the slippery member scored near the posts. Preston added a goal. Widnes were a thoroughly routed team in the later stages, and in quick succession Swift scored two tries, Fish in both instances adding the extra points. Final : Warrington, five goals seven tries (31 points) ; 'Widnes, one goal (two points).

Warrington P.S A. Society. The weekly meeting of the Warrington Society was held in the Co-operative Hall, Sankey-street, and was well attended. Mr. W. Wright presided, and gave a short address dealing with Christianity—its power and influence on modern society." Mr. D. Hatton, of Oldham, delivered an address on "lhe love of God." He pointed out that the greatest service a man could :ender to his Creator was " love." The highest ideal of life was to love God with all one's mind, heart and soul. Two solos were effectively rendered by Dliss Jessie Woodland, entitled " Daddy " and " The children's home." Mr. J. D. Gibson read the Scripture lesson. Mr. T. W. Wright and Mr. It. , Nelson also took part in the meeting.

"Heart's Desire" by Emerson Hough ; Mac- millan and Co.. Ss. It would probably require a considerable amount of guessing on the part of the average reader of fiction before he could hit on the meaning of the somewhat strange title Mr. Emerson Hough has given to his new novel. There are many things which different people might suggest as the " heart's desire" but in this case Heart's Desire " is the name of a little mountain town in New Mexico, wherein we have the scene of the story. At the time the narrative opens I"Heart's Desire" is a sort of Eyeless Eden where man I exists in a semi-civilized state 'free from the cares of ' family life,citizenship, and even the struggle for daily bread. The little town only boasts some 300 dollars combined capital, and the wealth of each single individual is dependent upon the proportion of this sum he holds at any one time. If he happens to have none, it does not matter much. The sun shines just the same, his friends are still friends, and by hanging up his gun behind the door of Uncle Ji'm Brothers', hotel " he can go on "tick" until such, time as he comes into a share of the floating dollars. There are some characters in the place more than ordinarily interesting and Mr. Hough's delineations of Curly, the " cow-puncher," Um Osby, the carrier, and Dan Anderson, the local "lawyer " and one- time graduate of Princetown, are masterpieces in , their way. -Most of the men have drifted to "Heart' Desire "because there has been a woman in the case sometime, and of course woman comes again. First we have the "littlest girl" from Kansas whose part is a subsidiary one. Then Eastern capital learns that there is gold and coal at " Heart's Desire " and brings Constance Ellsworth in its train. Romance has no* begun and Dan Anderson becomes our hero. He is the man in possession, the leader of the local cowboys, and Eastern capital finds it can do nothing without his help. How nobly the young man behaves under strong temptation, how he has, as he thinks, relinquished all chance of 2 ever making Constance his wife, and how, in the end, all comes right, form a charming story of great freshness and originality. It is full of quaint talk, dry cowboy humour, and not without a touch of pathos. Mr. Emerson Hough has struck a new line and the reader will follow it with interest right to the end. " Yolanda," by Charles Major ; Macmillan and Co., Oa. _ _

One of the most spirited and romantic ' novels we have read for some time is "Yolanda," Mr Charles Major's love-story of the daughter of Charles the Bold of Burgundy. It teems with interesting sitintions from first to last and is,moreover,so gracefully written as to possess an attraction in this respect which is none too common in modern fiction. It is no new thing in fiction for a gallant youth to lose his heart to a fair maiden, of whose identity he is for a long time in ignorance, and who utilises her knowledge to torment him most pleasantly. Maximilian of Hapsburg is scarcely the beau-ideal of knighthood. He is a good, honest youth, naturally handsome and strong as a lion, but his character-drawing is rather of to-day than of the times of romantic chivalry. Yolanda is, indeed, one of the most charming heroines who ever tripped daintily across the pages of historical romance. She is a creature of many pretty moods, none more alluring than the one in which, rigidly repressing her own identity, she endeavours to win Max's love for herself, and not for her position. Yolanda is in reality Mary, daughter lof that turbulent Prince, Charles the Bold of Burgundy, but she loves to be away with a good, honest merchant and his family, living the simple life, and it is in the guise of a burgher-maid that Max first meets her. Max had originally set out on a pilgrimage with the avowed object of wooing Mary of Burgundy and bodly demanding her hand from her adventurous father. His scruples are severaly tested by the alluring attractions of the fictitious Yolanda. However, in the end the path of love runs smooth. The machinations of foes are overcome by deeds of daring and political finesse, and Mr. Major carries his story to a triumphant conclusion. A number of dainty illustrations enhance the attractiveness of the book, which is worthy of a place among the best semi-historical romances. WHERE THE ELECTRO-MOTOR SCORES. We risk a lot in these days, says " Popular Elec- tricity." We always did before, but more depends upon it now than then. In industrial circles, for instance, how much hangs on the engine keeping up speed, turning regularly and constantly during working hours the wheels of .the busy mill or noisy workshop. Risks increase in proportion to the complexity of the apparatus and the number of moving tram!. An engine, for instance, whether steam, gas, or oil, is complicated, because it can only be made to do, ,by roundabout methods, what an electric motor does direct. The engineer wants rotary motion; but with steam, gas, and oil he must first have reciprocating motion (push and pull, so to speak), and this he converts into rotary motion by means of piston, connecting rod, and crank. The engineer has always done it that way, because it was the best for his purpose. Now, we have every respect for the engineer and his engine, but Ron% take chances with him or it. If you have to keep a shop going, and are depending on a gas, oil, or steam engine, you are taking chances, and we think you should shift your ground. You want rotary motion to drive your drills, and lathes and boring mills, so why not get direct, pure unadulterated revolutions per minute. The electric motor has no humbug about it in shape of valves, pipes, cylinders cranks, and what not. It is just what t was intended i to be—a rotating business member with a , pulley attached for a strap. It doesn't buck when you I look at it, and it won't" back fire." In a quiet corner of your shop, where the oil barrel now stands for your engine, it will stand, and do all the work and more than that steam or gas engine of yours. A VOICE WORTH DIVE THOUSAND A YEAR. Writing in the cyarnt "Windsor " on a fifth series of thirty-one" Vafflfry Fair "cartoons, which are finely reproduced in the original colours, Mr. F. Fletcher Robinson says "There is no more distinguished barrister Upon my list than Sir Henry Hawkins, to give him the title by which he was widely known for many years. He was never an oratorio the high-flown sense. Men said that he could not cross-examine, until Mr. Baigent came before him ; also they declared that he did not work at his briefs, until his masterly summary of the Tichborne case proved how he had laboured over and sifted the immense mass of evidence. He was ever quick at seeing the weakness of his opponent, as a born general should be, whether he is marshalling his evidencs or his armies. Withal, he had the drollest and most irresistible manner and, perhaps, the hoarsest voice extant ; indeed, he is stated to have said that his voic,) was worth five thou- sand a year to him. "One of most dramatic scenes ever remembered in a court of law occurred when Mr. Justice Hawkins was passing the sentence of death on a young woman convicted of the murder of her infamous lover. It was a glorious summer's day. The window of the court stood open, and in a hawthorn tree below a thrush was sing- ing. In the gloomy silence each note thrilled through the spectators, as if in the joy of the bird there was something uncanny. The judge had been presented with a bouquet of roses. These he bad in one hand. In the otigsr he held a knife with which the murder had, been codfinittecl. With his black cap on his trey head, he passed the sentence, usseverating each point with a movement of the knife or of the roses. That his heart was against his task was most plain. Indeed, the woman was subsequently respited and sentenced to imprisonment. But the whole scene—thrush, roses, knife, and judge—was most striking and remarkable." l'he April Windsor Magazine "is a very notable - te Original Cocoa, - and a Speciality.
