div.head: "PENNY GAFF" IN THE EAST END.
div.p: A "PENNY GAFF" IN THE EAST END.

It was a rather quixotic enterprise that a London woman of leisure undertook of late, when she went down to the East End to see if all the current accounts of its misery were true. Some of them she confirms, and others she denies in s chatty and very womanly article which appears in the April number of the "Pall Mall Magazine." But her narrative of the poverty and privation around her is relieved in one part by a comical description of a "penny gaff," which was the only amusement she discovered in the whole of the district of Poplar, Canning Town,and the parts adjacent. This is her account:—

I "Silence, lidies and gentlemen!" said a commanding voice—and the hubbub quieted down. A small man with long greasy hair brushed back artistically, a bushy moustache, and pale perspiring face, wearing an old frock-coat and trousers, with a gigantic sham-diamond pin stuck in his flaming red scarf, came and faced the crowd, and made the following breathless announce- ment :
" Lidies and gentlemen, I 'ave now the Honour of hintroducing to you the Dandy Dwarfs hengaged at henormoas hexpense for a farewell visit previous to their departure for the Continent. . _

Saying this,he pulled back the curtains and there on the stage were the flee celebrities. They were supposed ito be freaks of the Barnum order, but n reality were only undersized children" faked up " for the occasion. Yet I did not observe a doubting look nor hear an incredulous word during the ten minutes of the per- formance.

"They 'ave no deformity of any kind, like some so- called freaks "—here the Count turned slowly tound. "There ! yer see, tidies and gentlemen. (Order there, behind !—you two lidies with the red 'ats). This gentleman on the left is the son of the late General Tom Thumb,as he pointed out a tiny boy, also rigged up in a miniature suit of , evening dress. "He is married to this tidy " (another small child in pink satin and teeming with precious stones). " She is better known as the Princess Pawlyner, a Dutch lidy of noble birtb, but is also called he Human Doll I Site is now nine- teen years of age. This hinteresting couple was married last St. Patrick's Da v at the parish church in the street, Stratford. 'Er 'usband now stands beside 'is widdered mother ! " As he uttered this last fact his voice shook with emotion. _ .

The widowed mother was the centre of the group, a tiny little figure arrayed in black satin, and wearing a widow's cap over a grey wig. A pair of black spectacles and a respirator (the atmosphere was stifling !) covered sufficient of the child's face to prevent detection. The showman led her impressively to the front of the stage. With dramatic solemnity, he told us : " Phis, lidies and gentlemen, is the renowned Minnie Enderson, widow of the late General Tom Thumb, who 'as happeared on several occasions before her lite Mejjesty, Queen Victoria, an' hall the Rile Family. 'Er nime is known everywhere the Henglish langwidge is spoke, Larst Toosday being the 28th of November, was 'er birthday, she is therefore now in 'er 72nd year? The Count and Countess will now eralk through the haujence for hinspection l"—Here the noble couple were lifted off the platform, and went round the semi-circle cleared among the crowd, shaking bands. Poor mites! They ought to have been in bed hours before, and I saw more than one pathetic little yawn as they went through their parts.

div.head: OUTDOOR LIFE IN THE TWO CITIES.
div.p: OUTDOOR LIFE IN THE TWO CITIES.

The public life of Paris is lived by aliclasses from the richest to the poorest, and that causes the public Institutions to be not only more numerous, but more representative. In London, on the contrary, the public life is lived only by the poor, and iit is not a substraction from, but an nadequate sub- stition for the home life which is lived by those who can afford to possess it. Thus in this great feature there is a whole world of difference. The people of Paris care for their public buildings simply because they form a necessary part of their daily lives. The people of London tolerate them because it is only .a small part, and then, too, by a very free choice, of their lives. There are practically no clubs in Paris, while in London they abound, forming the concealed and limited public life which Londoners allow themselves to lead. Ie Paris one always feels that one sees and knows the place through and through. In London there are always the drawn blinds and the shutters behind which tale may not penetrate, and which give to the city an air of desolation and perhaps tnystery which,though possessing a charm of its own, is not pleasing to any but the most contemplative of minds. See how furiously quick the Londoner is to got away from the theatre night after night • the long stream of hurrying carriages and cabs whieh:follow on the closing of the places of amuse- ment are quick with the throbbing desire to get home away from the glare of light, away from the hum of public life. Driver and horse seem to share the quickened feeling, and there is perhaps no better means of know- ing what London really is than to watch and study this phenomenon of the night. It does not occur in Paris. After the theatre comes the supper or other form of enjoyment; and if this does not happen, the movement towards home is altogether a different aspect from what it is in London* It is more collective. Groups of people, rather than individuals or separated families, travel back, and the whole aspect of the occasion is quite eifferent.—From " A new TRIO of Two Cities," in the "Cornhill Magazine" for April.

div.head: STOCKTON HEATH TREEPLANTING. LIVELY PARISH MEETING. Amusing Speeches and Interruptions. DR. PARKEIS-: SERMON."
div.p: STOCKTON HEATH TREE- PLANTING. LIVELY PARISH MEETING. Amusing Speeches and Interruptions. DR. PARKEIS-: SERMON."
tended

course would have been to have widened the footpaths before planting the trees upon them. Footpaths were primarily intended to be walked npon—(" Hooray" and laueehter)—and not for trees to be planted upon them. If such obstructions were offered by human beings they would be removed by the police. I don't think the Parochial Committee hits a right to encroach upon narrow footpaths and not allow sufficient space for people to walk along them. Any local resident would be within his right in taking the law into his ownhands and removing trees which cease obstructions, and could, if hurt, successfully claim damages. (Laughter.) What would the Local Government Board think of public 1 money being collected with the object of placing unneces- sary obstructions in the village. We have a perfect The residents of Stockton Heath who ate_ strong force at the annual Parish Meeting in the Hall right to ask that the trees should be removed. div.head: Examiner, Saturday, March 31, 1906.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, March 31, 1906.

I shall give you a sermon. (Laughter.) lam one of those who believe that preaching comes a great deal by practice, and probably there are some hereto-night who believe that practice—that is to say medical practice— comes a great deal by preaching. (Laughter.) If that is so, don't forget me when you get the influenza— (laughter)—and should your senses get deranged by the sight of some unoffending tree, don't go on to Winwick, but call at my dispensary—(laughter)—where I shall administer to you some soothing balm, but more prob- ably a bitter drug to restore your distracted brain. (Laughter.) You all know' my brethren, for that is the term under which I intend to lump you all to-night in my capacity as clergyman, you all know there is no assembly, not even this, where there are not at least a few sinners—(laughter)—and I am delighted with the certainty of that fact—(loud laugh ter)—for I have strong faith that those sinners who have come here to scoff will go home to pray. (Hear, hear and laughter.) Now, my brethren, not being a pro- fessional but only an amateur parson, being a mere I beginner, having entered as it were only the infant school of preaching, not competing in the race with I those who can claim a direct Apostolic descent, I shall in consequence adopt very simply lines. I shall divide my text therefore into two heads (A Voice: Three, and laughter.) It is, I believe, the practice of professionals to divide their subjects into three heads and some into live, but should I adopt the larger number my heads I would undoubtedly become addled—(laughter)—and you would say I had lost ray own head with which ' nature has adorned me. (Laughter.) Coming to my two heads, we have first the belief of those who are with the Stockton Heath Tree Planting Com- mittee. We have the text " Let everyone be able to give a reason for the hope that is within him." That is my text ; these are its two divisions—the hopes of believers and the impertinent interference with the business of others, the prejudice and perversity of non- believers. (Laughter). What are the hopes of those who believe in the tree planting scheme of Stockton Heath ? We believe that those trees are efficacious in bringing health and contentment, beauty and prosperity to Stockton Heath. (Applause.) Who are these non- believers? I have mentioned their character. Do you wish their names (" Yes "). They are Mr. Ratepayer, I Mr. Another Ratepayer, Mr. Vigilant, Mr. Native, Mr. I Another Native, Mr. Faddist, and Mr. Cock of the , Walk. (Laughter.) These are the gentlemen who hav- ing eyes see not, who having legs walk crookedly. (Laughter.) I hope to-night they may meet with an obstruction. (Laughter.) It might be urged with reason that he who is so hopelessly inane RS to have no delight in the proximity of the trees is not worth the time or the expense which is necessary for his conver- sion. (Laughter.) But you must remember the Scrip- tural passage which says : "Charity suffereth long and is kind." I have to confess that it takes no small dose of charity to cure some of these obstructors. Brethren, if it is a crime to have participated in the labours of the Stockton Heath Tree-Planting Society, then I am the blackest criminal in all this district. (Laughter.) But believe me, were the whole community ranged against me in hostility to what I have done, and should they vow that they would blow the last am of soy anatomy into space, I should still think that what I had done was in order to confer a public service. (Loud applause.) I have stated In house after house where I have gone that it was for the people that I laboured, that it was for the public and not for an individual end. May not a man be self-sacrificing once in his life without his actions being questioned as having some selfish and ulterior end? Nay, my brethren, it makes me smile at the wretchedness of an opposition whose paltry spirit has been instigated by a a fictitious and hypocritical wrong. (Laughter.) The curse of some natures is hypocrisy. It would indeed be an interesting study to enter into the psychology of the motives of those who have raised objections to the scheme. Some object to trees from the fact that they have not put forth leaves, some because of the fact that they are not fruit trees—(laughter)—and there are even some gentlemen who have raised objection from the fact that the trees don't produce jam tarts and treacle toffee. (Loud laughter.) Now brethren, the objectors to this scheme should be divided into two classes —those who would not plant trees on footpaths less than six feet wide and those who would not plant them on footpaths 'less than eight feet wide. As to those who would not allow trees on footpaths less than 8 feet wide, these are the gentlemen who must denude your whole parish of all the trees planted in it except in Grappenhall-road. Is this a thing you would submit to ? (Cries of "No.") When I think that ignorance must be summoned to palliate that offence, lam reminded of the words of Bret Harte. I ask myself: Do I sleep, do I dream, Do I wonder and doubt Are things what they seem? Or is visions about? Is our civilization a failure Or is the Caucasian played out. (Laughter.) Away with petty prejudice ; fer it is due to the innate, perverse, contumacious, knotted, cross-grained intellects, the tomfooleries and antics of these gentlemen who are seemingly so doubly-dosed with original sin that they would drive poor Adam out of Paradise and wrest sweet Eve from her ambrosial bed. (Great laughter.) These are the gentlemen who are the opponents of the scheme and I say it is this which has urged me to give you a sermon to-night in order to strengthen the faint-hearted who are inclined to lose faith in this scheme. (Loud applause.) COUNCILLOR PEMBERTON HAS A WORD. Councillor Pemberton moved an amendment to the effect that trees which were planted in inconvenient places should be removed. Mr. Westbrook agreed to add a similar clause to his resolution. Councillor Pemberton said all present were in favour of the scheme; it was only a question of where the trees should be planted. The village was under a great debt of gratitude to Dr. Parker—(applause) —for the energetic and able manner in which he bad worked for the scheme. There could be no doubt that some trees were planted in inconvenient positions. He suggested that permis- tion might have been obtained to plant trees on the canal side. Dr. Parker's arguments appeared to him something like bringing an 81 ton gun to kill a fly. (Laughter.) He was afraid the trouble had started not so much between the Tree Planting Committee and some one else as between one or two members of the Parochial Committee. Mr. Whitley had been elected time after time by the ratepayers and he possessed the confidence and respect of a certain number of the in- habitants. He had only been voicing the opinions of ratepayers who had spoken to him and it was his duty to do that. It was suggested that the resolution should be amended to read that trees which in the opinion of the Surveyor were dangerous or inconvenient should be removed, but Councillor Pemberton said that would be unfair to Mr. Swinton. Councillor Lord said he thought they could all agree to the resolution. He would be sorry to see any adverse vote taken against Mr. Whitley who, he believed, had acted as he considered in the best interests of every- body. They thought certain trees had been put in the wrong places and now that they were going to be removed they could support the resolution which was not a condemnation of Mr. Whitley or anyone else. Mr. IL J. Westbrook said they all recognised that the footpaths on whick trees were planted would not be so wide as they were before the planting. As they were all agreed that the trees should not be in objec- tionable places he thought the petition was unnecessary He defied anyone to state that they had made objections to the Tree Planting Committee which had not received consideration. As sensible men they recognized they ' would have to suffer a little inconvenience and they were prepared to suffer to that extent. (Applause.) I It was suggested that Mr. Whitley should allow the petition to remain in abeyance pending the satisfying of the objectors by the Tree Planting Committee It was um'erstood that Mr. Whitley would take this course, and the resolution as amended was unanimously approved. It read: "This meeting approves the tree- planting scheme, but suggeats that in places where any ' particular tree or trees nr,guard shall in the opinion of the Tree Planting Committee be in dangerous or incon- venient positions, the same shall be remedied or they ' shall be removed." A vote of thanks to the chairman for presiding con- cluded the meeting.

treated the matter seriously and wished it to be dealt with in a business like manner, for the other speakers poured forth as much ridicule as they possibly could upon " objections." The resolution which was unanimously carried, like the meeting, was farcical, for the objections to certain trees have been left in the hands of the Tree Planting Committee to deal with—seeing that they planted them. The committee are left in the position of Defendants, Judge, and Jury, and so it is expeoted the 'verdict will be Not Guilty." It would have been much better to have left these matters in the hands of the District Surveyor—We hope the trees will flourish and cease to annoy and as Dr. Parker said bring health and contentment to the Heathens.

The goals were scored by W. H. Banks and W. Richardson. The score does not indicate the game in the least, as seldom did the Bankfield team manage to get the ball over the half-way line. The visitors goal keeper was practically a spectator, not being called upon to save one single shot.
The second eleven visited the Royal club, and although minus three of their regular team, managed to win by 2-1. The goals were scored by H. Owen and L. Pierpoint.
This week Stockton Heath conclude the season, when the first eleven Nviß visit Bebington, while the second go to Frodsham.
The following teams have been chosen to represent Stockton Heath :

Ist eleven (at Bebington)—R. G. Pierpoint, goal ; E. E. Woods and E. Pierpoint (captain) backs ; J. G. Hatton, H. Kirkconnell, and Eric Fairclough, halves ; H. Dolan, W. Richardson, W. H. Banks, and S. Baxter, forwards. Train leaves Central Station 1.50. Referee, W. Carter. .

• 2nd (at I, rodsham)—F. G. Kartland, goal; B.Silcock and P. B. Ilawtin (captain) backs ; H. Smith, E. Jones and B. Guest, halves ; E. Fairclough, A. Hodgkinson, H. Owen, 1. Day and J. Houghton, forwards. Train leaves Bank Quay 2.30. Referee, N. W. Bellamy.

NATIONAL INSURANCE. VICE-ADMIRAL MANN AND ENGLANDS' DEFENSIVE FORCES. Lecture to the Warrington Chamber of Commerce. A meeting of the Warrington Chamber of Commerce was held at the Town Hall on Tuesday evening at which I Vice-Admiral Mann delivered an address on the need for National Insurance. The President of the Chamber, Councillor Fulton Smith, presided and there was an excellent attendance. Councillor FULTON SMITH pointed out that traders and manufacturers protected their trade, property, and men under them by means of insurance, and the rate- I payers insured against burgulary &c., by maintaining a police force. What was good for the individual in that direction he thought was also good for the nation. If it was necessary for tho individual to protect his interests it was necessary for the nation to safe- guard her's, botk within the boundaries of the country and on the high seas—within the country by a well equipped and standing army and on the high seas by a strong navy. They must not loose sight of the fact that there was no standing still. All nations were strengthening themselves and many bad aspirations to acquire land and power throughout the universe. Naturally in their aspirations they looked towards the richest country and there was no doubt that we were the envy of the world. That being so we must not rest content with the present condition of affairs but must use every effort and every argument to impress upon those in authority the necessity of maintaining the superiority and efficiences of our national defensive rescources. (Applause). Vice-Admiral MANN said the ownership of a vast empire brought with it responsibilities to civilization to manage the empire property and to defend it. What had England got to defend her property? First of all there was the navy and there were no two opinions about it, that many had to be over- whelmingly strong and absolutely efficient. They were constanly being told that the navy was going to the dogs but they must not believe it. Never had there been a time when the navy was so abso- lutely efficient as it was at the present moment, owing to the drastrio changes which had been made by Admiral Sir John Fisher' and they could say" Let, em all come" but not more than two at a time. He hoped they would rest content that for the present the navy was supreme though he was not prepared to say how long it would remain so. We had built a now warship which was going to revolutionise matters and we had preserved the secret of the ship. If that vessel was a success we would follow with a squadron of the same type and would to that extent be Jahead of the other nations. (Hear, bear.) He felt very much for his brother officers an the sister service as they had always had over them some Heaven-born civilian minister who came into office with the experience of the oldest general. (Laughter) The wonderful part about the army was that it was in such a state of efficiency at present in spite of that system. The present Minister for War, Mr. Haldane, he was glad to say, was an absolutely different type of man, who would think the questions out and who would rely upon the advice of the experts. He thought nothing but good could come of Mr. Haldane's control of affairs. The regular army so far as it went was good. With regard to the reserve forces, having regard to the extent of their training, they were excel- lent. He had seen some well trained volunteer regi- ments and some officers of the volunteers who were fit , to take command anywhere, but as a general rule the volunteers were not so good. He had always wondered why it was that some 12,000 or 13,000 patriotic men should do something behind which millions of their unpatriotic fellow-countrymen sheltered. In the volun- teers they had the best material they possibly could have if they could only train them sufficiently. But they could not expect the volunteer to give more time, and the short time they did give was not enough to train them to stand against really trained soldiers. He was a man of peace, and as such said that if we wanted peace we must he prepared for war. Behind our regular army we must have a greater expan- sion. How were they to bring that about ? The volun- teers were not sufficient and a man of common sense would at once agree with that, but when a form of universal training was advocated they immediately said it was the thin end of the wedge of conscription. Con- scription was not possible because it was the people's business and the people would not have it. They believed that voluntary effort would not do and there- fore proposed that boys at school should be taught military drill and trained to the use of the rifle, to be followed by further training. Vice Admiral Mann pro- ceeded to advocate a national system of military train- ing on the lines proposed by the National Service League on the ground that it would improve the physique and morale of the nation. They were told that invasion of England was impossible but there were situations to be imagined when our navy might be away for a few days. At the time of the Dogger Bank incident it would have taken four days for the fleet to have been concentrated in those waters and a great deal could happen in four days. With such a force as as re h pea r eewsash otuhled best t preparedmeans of of r wa r,a n securingcl peace. Besides securing our national peace, it would prepared for proposedwar we be of tremendous advantage in other ways. To bring this about ranch spade work needed to be done, and the National Service League was established for that , purpose. If the principle was once established that the youth of this country should go in for this training, then the whole problem was solved. This was the nation's business, and if the whole nation had to pre- pare itself to go out and fight, they would take jolly good care that the Government did not make war rashly. (Applause.) Mr. A. J. JOLLEY, in proposing a vote of thanks to Vice-Admiral Mann, said he had given them a great deal to think about. Much he had said would, perhaps, not commend itself in all points to detail to everyone present, hut from the general trend of his remarks on national insurance, scarcely anypne in the room would venture to differ. Anyone yab reflected upon the tremendous issues involved must agree that not only the object that the Admiral and Lord Roberts had in view, but the methods by which they proposed to achieve that object were in the highest degree desirable. Their object was not merely to secure national insurance in any narrow or material sense. English people had been the pioneers of progress for the whole of the human race, and our highest glory in the future would be that the name of England should be associated with freedom and progress,and the carrying of blessings to the lower races of mankind. (Applause). Colonel EDELSTEN in seconding gave several examples from history to show that immunity from aggression from outside could not be safely relied upon. The sky might not be clouded at present. they one did not on that account throw away their umbrellas. The tail that might be said to be wagging the dog in Parliament now believed that all these things could be got over by international fraternity. Exactly the same thing was said in 1851, at the time of the great Exhibi- tion, but since then there had been no less than 14 great wars, an average of one great war every four years, and yet it was said that with the interchange of commodi- ties and all that sort of thing there was to be no more war. The origin of war was to be found in the desire of possession, and had there been any shrinkage in that , respect ? It was to the interior of the human heart one I mnet look if one wished to see any indication of the ending of war. He submitted there never was chola a time as the present irt which men were so determined to possess themselves of the last halfpenny that could be got hold of. (Laughter and applause). The resolution was heartily carried. Alderman BENNETT, in proposing a vote of thanks to the Chairman, and to the Mayor for the use of the room, said apologies had been received for non-attend- ance from the Mayor. Sir Gilbert Greenall. Colonel Pilkington. Colonel Walker and Mr. J. C. Parr. He explained that the meeting was in no sense political. It was purely and solely a meeting of the Chamber of Commerce, and was the result of the able speech Lord Roberts delivered in London a few menths ago, and more recently in Liverpool, showing koty important it was from a commercial point of view that the matter should be taken up, and they had done so. (Applause.) Mr. C. E. PARKER seconded, and the motion was carried, the CEIAIRMAN briefly returning thanks.

div.head: NOTES ON THE STOCKTON HEATH
div.p: NOTES ON THE STOCKTON HEATH
MEETING.

The Stockton Heathens evidently went to the meet- ing for fun—and they got it. From the tone of the meeting one gathered all pre- sent were in favour of "Tree planting' and niore than one was anxious to claim himself "Father of the Lryers", the Law i scheme." More than one, too, took the Opportunity as "Amateur Law Ltualsweyretirssin,,g hainmds parnodf szenraall p being freely bandied about, as f it were a shuttle- cock. Another gentleman took upon himself the role of minister and said he would preach a sermon and began by addressing tie audience as "My Brethren." The oratory too at times was something out of the common and it was not surprising that the reporters' pencils needed sharpening more than once, as the language was most lurid and imaginative. 1 The meeting too disclosed that a forensic wonder 1 dwells in their midst, for Dr. Parker showed in no unmistakeable fashion at time that be is possessed of the natural characteristics of some of his race, viz. oratorical powers', humour and word painting though perhaps he was carried away at times with the exuberance of his own verbosity. Councillor Pemberton who followed Dr. Parker , said the latter's speech appeared to him like "an Si ton gun attacking a fly." Mr. Whitley had prepared himself with a list of the accidents that had occurred, but as he rt a I them, the audience would not seriously listen to them, for they simply shrieked with laughter, especially over one relating to a young lady, " whose garments" be said "became entangled in the guard around the tree and she had to be assisted out., _ .
_ Probably, of the speakers, only Messrs. Hough, Whitley, Sherburne, Brown, Lord and Pemberton

div.head: • NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: • NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
RUGBY FOOTBALL.
By " Ovalist."

The question of the hour at Wilderspool on Saturday was whether Mr. Tom King was a referee or a humorist. I should say, myself, that he was both. Some of his decisions were a trifle late, but they were always fair. Once, for instance, he gave Warrington a penalty kick when they were really the offenders,but ho quickly atoned for the slip by awarding poor, down- trodden Widnes a penalty right in front of the p 'Fits which resulted in a goal. There was a distinct air of sympathy about it, and Mr. King's perpetual, amiable smile seemed a trifle broader than usual. He is not one of the strict, ever-whistling type of referee and the game was none the worse for his leniency in regard to knock-on and other small infringements. In a serious cup-tie, however, it is conceivable that there might be Itrouble unless Mr. King were a trifle more solemn in aspect and severe in administration.

I had the presumption to say last week that War- rington would start winning again on Saturday when Widnes were the visitors. It has not been often this season that I could venture to predict a result with any certainty, but this time I had an easy target and scored a " bull " first shot. Notwithstanding their misfortunes, Warrington have not deteriorated to the extent that the Widnes men have. Their reserves are of a superior calibre, and though only two of the backs who fought ia the Cup-final turned out on Saturday, the team was sufficiefitly strong to beat Widnes by a huge total of 5 goals, 7 tries (31 points), to one goal (2 points). This, I should say, is the biggest- licking Warrington ever gave their near neighbours.and from present appearances there is small chance of Widnes ever getting even with the " Wire - pullers." There was no comparison between the teams, but Widnes might have kept the score down if they had not given up the ghost so early.

The score is rather flattering to Warrington, for the home team did not play the brilliant football that such prolific scoring would suggest. There was a lot of raggedness in the display of the backs and combina- tion never reached the standard one expects from Warrington. Most of the be work was individual, some of it being very clever. At half we had two men who had neTer played together before and both were " outside " men, so that the understanding was generally rather mixed. Lambert and Lees both did some smart things, and the former justified his trial. With experience he will develop, and there was more than one glimpse of the personal trickiness which has been conspicuous in his "A " team work. With a good scrummage half to feed him, he would, I think, do even better. A tendency to recklessness in his passing was the worst fault he displayed.

-- A word of praise is due to the forwards, who gave a fine display in all departments. They had quite a day out in the scoring line, and no less than five of the tries came to them, often after smart hand to hand passing. Thomas and Swift each got two, and were always to the fore. Jordan was a better centre than Isherwood, who frequently did the wrong thing and had quite an " off ' day. Fish obliged with a try in quite his old style, but is obviously short of training. Harris played very poorly, but Berry at full back was high-class throughout. The same may be said of Tilley, his vis-l-vis who was the ouly man on the Widnes side to do anything of note.

There were several big scores put up on Saturday, and two teams at least, Halifax and Salford, deserve penalising for playing practically a reserve side at Oldham and Bradford. This sort of thing is unfair to the public, and the Northern Union ought to put its foot down in the interests of good sport: Leigh maintained their leadership by winning somewhat luckily at St. Helens. They have only to play Huddersfield and Hull Kingston Rovers away now, and Oldham at home,ancl are almost certain champions.
The South-Nrest Lancashire League table up-to-date is as folloms Points.

A fortnight ago, by a curious freak of memory I stated in this column that Warrington would share the Leeds v. Broughton Rangers cup-tie gate, and I notice that on Saturday this "terminological inexacti- tude " had found its way into the " Football Chronicle." A moment's thought makes the error quite obvious. If Leeds had been due to play War- rington at Warrington on the date of the cup-tie they would have had to share the gate, but as the fixture was at Leeds the Warrington Club was involved in no loss by the cup-tie. It is a pity the League engagment was not at Warrington, for the gate at Leeds realised over .£5OO. This would be divided by Leeds and the Rangers.

To-day, Warrington are due again at Rochdale, where they have already won once this season—in the Lancashire Cup They should repeat the performance, even though the Hornets' team has been strengthened since October. Warrington will be almost at full strength again, for Hockenhall, Dickenson, and Board- man all return to the Ride. I quite thought Dickenson would have had enough injuries to keep him at home for the rest of the season, but ho is pronounced fit and eager for the fray again.

The selected fifteen is as follows :-13erry, full back ; Fish, Isherwood, Dickenson and Taylor, three- quarters ; Hockenhall and Lees, half backs ; Preston, Boardman, Shugars, Thomas, Jolley, Heath, Swift and Harmer, forwards.

The ge'A " team returns to combination football to-day and should easily obtain a couple of points at the expense of the Hornets "A " team. Nothing is being left to chance, and the following strong twelvo have been selected: Knight, full-hack; Jordan, Cartwiight, Brooks and Kenyon, three-quarters; Lambert and Lloyd, half-backs; Ashton, Fairhurst, Forster, Bradshaw and Morrison, forwards.
Hockey. On Saturday last Stockton Heith first eleven visited Palliateld, and after a one sided grin, won by 2-0.

div.head: NATIONAL SERVICE LEAGUE.
div.p: NATIONAL SERVICE LEAGUE.

There was a good attendance at a meeting held at the Lion Hotel in the evening under the auspices of the Warrington Branch of the National Service Leaune. Mr. H. Roberts presided, and was supported by Vice- Admiral Mann, Colonel R. C. Winder (Bolton), Dr. W. J. Collins and Captain Crosfleld. The CutAinMk.N said without hesitation that the more the conditions which obtained in England were con- sidered, and the more the principles of the National

Service League were thought over, the more likely it I was that those people who gave time to the considera- tion of those two matters would become strong and enthusiastic advocates of the principles they were met to espouse. (Applause). These principles inculcated the very highest form of patriotism, and he believed they were counsels of prudence and commonsense. He denied that the principles of the League involved con- scription or anything like it. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Vice-Admiral MANN then delivered an interesting address.

Speeches followed from Colonel Winder, Dr. Collins, Mr. J. H. Smethurst, Mr. G. Dale and Mr. John Darbyshire the latter a whom dissented from the pro- visions of League as being at variance with the laws of the Prince of Peace.

div.head: Another Plea for Paving.
div.p: Another Plea for Paving.

Sir,—Permit me, through your columns, to draw the attention of the Paving Committee to the discreditable state of the back passage between Willis-street and Algernon-street. In wet weather it is over ankle-deep in mud, and in some parts there are pools of water six to eight inches deep. No wonder that there is so much sickness amotrist the children in the neighbourhood. These two streets have now been in existence eight or nine years, and what is difficult to understand is that other streets in the vicinity, though of much later date in construction have been paved for some time. Resi- dents of Willis-street and Algernon-street are under the impression that by some accidental oversight this passage has been omitted from the schedule of the Paving Committee. Perhaps one of the Fairfield Ward representatives who are on this committee will kindly make inquiries to see if this ialthe case, and if so, to press the paving forward for early attention.—Y ours A PARENT.

div.head: Recent Drowning Fatality.
div.p: The Recent Drowning Fatality.

Sir,—Will you kindly allow me through the -columns of your paper to refer to the recent drowning of my son Arthur in the canal at Bewsey. With a view to making an endeavour to prevent a recurrence of such a painful accident, I should take it as a special favour if any of your readers can inform me. (1). Whether life buoys are supposed to be placed on the Turn Bridges along the Canal, and, (2). If any of the Lock keepers understand, or are supposed to understand artificial respiration. I ask these questions for the sake of humanity, as from my own painful experience,if a life buoy had been handy, or if artificial respiration had been resorted to when my boy was recovered from the canal, instead of being left, as he was, on the bank,l am firmly convinced from information I have since obtained, my son would I have been restored to us.

As there have been a good many drowning cases lately and as you cannot stop children from going near the Canal, is it not time that something should be done in the way of placing Life saving apparatus on the Canal Bridges, or at convenient places along the Canal, even if we cannot expect that all canal officials shall understand first aid to the drowning.--I remain yours faithfally, JJ J. FAIRHURST. 68, Tanners Lane, Warrington, March 28th.

div.head: School of Art Headmaster.
div.p: School of Art Headmaster.

Sir,—Students of the School of Art have read with the greatest surprise as well as indignation the report of the proceedings of the Education Committee at its last meeting with reference to the Art Master (Mr. Aylward). Especially do we regret to see that the imputation of incapacity as a teacher was most unkindly and unfairly charged against him. As students of the school for various lengths of time, we desire to express our deep sympathy with the Master under such unjust condemna- tion, and assure him of our warm appreciation of his efforts co give us the best guidance in his power. While we state our views with some natural hesita- tion we cannot but feel that in one respect we have better opportunities for judging his work in the school than gentlemen, most of whom, however able, seldom— if ever—visit the school to judge for themselves. It would almost appear that unfair influences have been at work to undermine the position of a gentle- man whose thoughts are given to his work rather than to the up-to-date business methods of making safe his situation.

We trust that the authorities will see that justice is done to one with so long a record of honourable ser- vice to the town of Warrington. On behalf of 27 evening students of the school.— Yours, &0., HARRY SFIERBURN. T. B. WHITBY.

div.head: Rev. E. C. E. Carleton and Catholics.
div.p: Rev. E. C. E. Carleton and Catholics.

Sir,—Mr. Carleton strikes out a line for himself, for certainly no one appears to be so up-to-date, and from time to time he treats us to some of his most marvel- lous ideas. His latest effusion (March 23rd) is too funny, really. It is quite reasonable to expect the next thing we shall be told is that on account of their foreign allegiance the Catholics come under the Aliens' Act and must clear out of England. Just imagine the rush of emigrants to the Continent? It is too terrible to contemplate the tremendous gap that must eventually, be filled by more foreign labour. However, Mr. Carleton need not flatter I himself that " his Irish Nationalist friends " will accept his leadership in either spiritual or temporal matters, for his wild utterances will not be taken seriously, not even CUM grotto salis, but as a poor joke. Apparently, his knowledge of English history does not carry him far enough back to locate "the ancient Church lof the land," that is to say, its introduction. It was already ancient at his earliest date ; has never been quite annihilated; though all that he knows, and much that he has yet to learn of Christianity is in a more flourishing condition than ever, and must continue to flourish to the end of ti me,altho ugh its creeds, Ac. are not taught at Holy Trinity Church. Where was the teaching of Christianity more than 1,000 years ago to come from if not from Rome, its then settled home, and where was the need for adding the New Artioles"referred to previous to the advent of Protestantism ?The ancient churchen joys this distinct advantage : she has never subtracted nor may she subtract one inspired dogma for the temporal convenience of individuals.—Yours faithfully, J. W. CAVANAGFI. Golden Square Chambers, March 29th, 190 g.

div.head: ~ Fair Play's" Reply to the Rev. J. F. Matthews.
div.p: ~ Fair Play's" Reply to the Rev. J. F. Matthews.

Sir,—' must thank the Rev. J. F. Matthews for extend- ing to me the honour of being the first anonymous writer he has ever noticed, also for his fine but inaccurate definition of myself whom he classes as one who believes implicitly because I have so been taught. In reference to my signing anonymously, there are reasons apparent to the common layman why I deemed it advisable. In doing so, I maintain I have noted con- sistently with every code of honour, providing I made no personal attack upon the character of any individual or body. The rev, gentleman lays before us as his fundamental standpoint the Government returns of State grants made to the erection of Voluntary schools and on the strength of those returns denies us the right to class ourselves as " The man in possession." I give the figures for those who would like to study the the Catholic share of the pie. Church of England schools received £1,515,205. Roman Catholic_ schools received _59,579.

Unsectarlan- and Wesleyan received 201070. Side by side with those figures, we must place the following facts :—The building grant, which forms the Catholic obligation, extends over a period of 76 years. Many of those State assisted schools have become obso- lete, others having been erected in their place. The money was granted to assist voluntary efforts, to educate British Catholic subjects, and to save the State from incurring the whole cost. Another matter worthy of consideration is that we Catholics contribute our full share to the public purse, and for a period of 32 years we have not claimed any portion of the amount raised by local rates for educational purposes. If such is the I lease, and I stand open to correction, I maintain we have 1 settled the debt we owed to a generous State, and may II !justly claim the right of ownership to our schools. To I I advocate Sunday schools is no solution of the religious • difficulty. Many a child, poor in this world's riches, but proud in spirit,Would never hear the name of religion mentioned, simply because the question of Sunday I clothes would lay it open to the sneers of even Sunday I school scholars. Such a state of affairs is regrettable' but undeniable. My contention is that we must adhere' to the present religious system, or accept Secularism. As to the Government throwing over the present volun- tary schools and building fresh ones, the proposal will afford food for deep reflection to the already grumbling ratepayer who at the present time in War- rington is trying to solve the problem of " How to build a school at a cost of £lO per child." In with- drawing from this controversy to make room for better men, I must tender my thanks to the rev, gentleman for the courteous way he has replied to my letter.Speak- ' ing of myself, it has helped to educate me on both sides of the auestion. In conclusion my friend will forgive me if 1 recall an incident of last summer. Returning from enjoying the beauties of Hill Cliff° my wife and I had the pleasure of hailing the Rev. J. F. Matthews in one of his open-air discourses. If I remember right, he spoke of the belief in a nod, of the good influences of Christianity, and the hope that it • would make us all better men and women. It is to that hope we say Amen, with all our hearts. It is with that object in view we wish to keep religion in cur ' schools, claiming that right and not denying it to ' others. We all have the welfare of our children at
Sink

heart. It is our sole ambition that when we have passed beyond this vale of tear a they may become the good men and women of the/ 'me. With a view to meeting the wishes of my friend slave decided to drop • my non-de-plume of "Fair Play." Yours, FRANCI r. McGARTY, 21, Elaine-street, March 270, 1906.

div.head: Extension of Time Asked for.
div.p: Extension of Time Asked for.

In connection with the proposal to utilize the Warrington lay-by on the Manchester Ship Canal for local traffic, the Rivers Committee of the Corporation and the Lay-by Committee of the Chamber of Corn merce visited the new warehouse which is in the course of erection at Walton this (Friday) morning and were favourably impressed with the possibilities of the position. We understand that the Chamber of Commerce have approached the Ship Canal Company with a view to securing an extension of time for the construction of the Warrington Dock and pointing out the undesirability of covering the intended site (Arpley meadows) with the dredgings from the river. The Rivers Cou,mittee have passed a similar resolution and a deputation has been appointed to wait upon the Ship Canal Company with reference thereto.

div.head: Effect of the Sugar 0.-anvention.
div.p: The Effect of the Sugar 0.-anvention.

Sir,—ln previous correspondence on this subject I gotjthe impression from the style of the arguments used that those who supported this Convention were doing so, not so much because they believed in the Convention or had gauged its effects, but being Con- servatives they naturally desired to minimise the in- fluence which the results of the arrangement would have upon their party in theCelection then imminent. Now that the political issue has been settled for some time to come, it is possible for all to view the questiou from a commercial and national standpoint uninflu- enced by party considerations. The effect of the Convention may be summarized as follows:

First. The increased price has reduced our con- sumption of sugar. Second. The consumption amongst the Continental sugar producing countries who are signatories of the Convention has been increased as a result of the reduc- tion in price. Third. The number employed in the confectionery and allied trades has been reduced, according to the President of the London Chamber of Commerce, by 12,000. Fourth. We have been prevented from making good our shortage duo to the poor crop of 1904 from such countries as Russia, Argentine, and Spain. The general effect can best be gauged, not by the variations in our own pricei, but by comparison of the prices before and after the Convention in different lands. Let us take this country, and the countries of France Germany and Belgium from which we get large supplies. The following table giving the retail prices shews this at a glance. .

England Germany France Belgium per lb. per lb. per lb. per lb. Previous to Convention lid. 31d. 4')?d. 3.7 d. March Ist, 1905 2-2 d. 2d. 3vd. 27,d. March Ist, 1906 11d. 24d. 3d. 21d. It will be seen that we are paying 17 per cent, more for our sugar while these three countries are paying 38 per cent. less. , It is but fair to say that part of this difference is the 'effect of the Sugar Tax. But this tax is paid to our own Government while the bounties, abolished by our ico-operation, were practically gifts to this country. I The record crop of 1905 (presuming that the bounty Isystem had been undisturbed) would have reduced our Iprices to below those existing before the Convention. No one would object to continental users getting sugar at a low price, but why we should have gone out of our way to enter into a Convention which would prevent us getting cheap sugar it is difficult to say. We are not now concerned about this folly, except in so much that its results may be clearly realised, and that it may act as a warning to us not to adopt any form of retaliation which will have the effect, of increasing the price of the articles we import. In regard to the West Indies for whose benefit this mistake was made, the increase of our imports from this quarter is insignificant. The figures for January and February are just out, and our imports are 227,333cwt5., an increase of less than 4,ooocwt. on the previous year. From Germany alone we imported in the same period 3,109,644 cwt. Our Statesmen who entered into this Convention, on the ground that the West Indian planters were exposed to unfair Competition with bounty fed sugar adopted a method which raised the prices of 25 parts of sugar that one(the West Indian proportion) should be raised. In a word, in order that we might pay an extra half- penny to sugar growers in the West Indies we sacrificed two shillings which bounty giving countries were will- ing to give. Perhaps the greatest need of Statesmen and indeed of anyone,is an accurate appreciation of pro- portion. To wilfully sacrifice ten million pounds for the sake of giving £5OO to our colonists in the West Indies was an act of lolly the extent of which the British people should fully realise, so that whatever be the party name of the Government in power, such folly might never be repeated. CEIARLES E. PARKER. Penketh, March 27th, 1906.

div.head: ~ • RELIGIOUS INSTRUCTION. Canon Morley Stevenson and the Rev. J. F. Matthews.
div.p: ~ • RELIGIOUS INSTRUCTION. Canon Morley Stevenson and the Rev. J. F. Matthews.

At a meeting of Church parents at Hamilton-street on Monday, Canon Stevenson said his attention had been called to a letter written by the Rev. J. F. Matthews a gentleman for whom he had a very great respect. Mr. Matthews says i "I find ten of the schools in Warrington received £4,839 towards their erection; eight of these schools are Anglican. They cost £10,767 ;of this £7,112 was given in eub- scriptions, &c., while the remainder, £3,625, came from grants." Mr. Matthews had forgotten ono thing. He had got hold of an old Government Blue book.He did not know Warrington as well as he (Canon Stevenson) did, and had forgotten that some of the schools about which he was talking had been pplled down, and other schools put in their place. The new schools had received no building grants at all. The, old school of St. James' which faced Knutsford-road had been shut up as a school. There was a building grant on that, but there was no grant to the new school which had taken its place. So they must sub- tact certain schools which had either been pulled down or shut up, iii and remember that new schools had been built for which no Government grant had been given. It was quite true that many years ago the Government gave grants towards the building of schools,—they were very small—but they , gave those grants equally to all people, whether Church of England, Roman Catholics, or any other sect, and any body of people who wished to build a school could ~ i get a grant from the Government. Did they mean to , tell him that because the Government made a small grant—say £loo—towards their schools 40 or 50 years ago that they should not say it was their school, the Church of England school. If the Government were t I going to take such lines—ho did not think they would— all he could say was that the managers would put their hands into their pockets and give the Government their £lOO back. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Matthews went on to say "I wish the clergy would be quite frank with their congre- gations and reveal the whole facts. Neither Canon Stevenson, nor the clergy of his Church, nor the Roman Catholic clergy, have protested at all against the glar- ing injustice with which the Act of 1902-3 aims a deadly 1 Wow at the religious convictions of Free Churchmen." . He (Canon Stevenson) had always stood for perfectly fair play all round, and that they should have teaching according to their different beliefs. (Hear, hear.) He would be prepared to advocate such legislation as would* give in every place in the land religious teaching according to the desire of any number of parents. (Hear, hear.) This was not a question so much for the clergy or the school managers, but for the parents, and if they made it quite clear that they wished to have their children taught in the same way as themselves then he believed that their claim was so just that the Government could not refuse to listen to it. (Applause).

Lovely-lane residents will be pleased to learn tha the pipes for improving the water supply to the district have now arrived, and that the work of re-laying the mains will be commenced at an early date. Expenditure under the head of Education in War- rington has been so much discussed lately that the idea may be prevalent among the unenlightened that the teaching of the young is managed on extravagant lines. As a matter of fact this is far from being the case, and Warrington will compare very favourably with most towns in regard to the cost of education. Mr. Upson, president of the local Teachers' Association, gave some figures on Saturday which bear on the question of the cost of education and are worthy of inspection. The largest item, he said, was the teachers' salaries. We hear a good deal about the generous treatment of , teachers when the annual increases come round, but the average salary, including headmasters, is only 30s. per week. Mr. Upson proved—if proof were needed —that the tgachers are worth all they get and instanced the remarkable advance, in the quality of instruction given, since the Act of 1902. So far Warrington has managed to combine economy with educational effici- ciency, and if a means can be found of building new , schools on the reasonal4le basis of 10 per head there will not be much for the ratepayer to grumble about.

1906 Bicycles. Considerable change in the designs of machines are taking place this season. The path-racing man appears to have abandoned the idea of the forward dropped top tube, and path - raeing. machi are being generally ordered with true horizontal top tubes. But with light road-racing bicycles the forward dropped top tube. is tnore pronounced than ever. Large numbers of very light road-racing machines are also beina: built on similar lines to those of the bicycle 'affected by Mr. 011ey for the road. The special feature of these machines is that they have a 24-in, driving wheel and a 26-in. steering wheel. The object of having machines constructed' on these :tines is to ensure greater lightness without any loss of strength, and if the large numbers of trial machines of this class now being tUrned out give satisfaction, we shall, no, doubt, see this pattern pnerally adopted by all makers net season. New Ideas in Brakes. , The prese4 season is witnessing a change of opular fancy as - regards • brakes. Concealed brakes, either wholly Or partly inside the frame, seem to be giving place to different new lever brake' systems, where all the mechanism is outside the frame of the bicycle, and consequently easily accessible. Thus we seem to be gradually going oack to the old methods of applying brakes, except that by slight alterations of the old mechanism, the brakes are now made to apply to the rims of the bicycle, instead of to the tyres, as in the old days. 11/ .
